What Are Mutual Funds?

📅 27 May 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list.
  • This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.
  • In a recent development, A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list. They are one of the most widely used investment vehicles in the country, and for good reason. But not all mutual funds are built the same, and understanding the differences can have a real impact on how much money you actually keep over time.

This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.

In a recent development, A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle. When you invest in a mutual fund, your money is combined with money from thousands of other investors. A fund manager then uses that pool of capital to buy a collection of assets, which might include stocks, bonds, or a mix of both, depending on the fund’s objective.

According to recent reports, each investor owns shares of the mutual fund, and those shares represent a proportional stake in everything the fund holds. When the underlying assets increase in value, your shares go up. When they fall, your shares go down.

Mutual funds are priced once per day, after the market closes, based on the total value of all the assets inside the fund. This is called the net asset value, or NAV. Unlike stocks, which trade throughout the day at constantly changing prices, mutual fund transactions are always settled at the end-of-day price.

Sources indicate that when you buy shares of a mutual fund, you are not picking individual stocks or bonds yourself. Instead, you are hiring a fund manager, or a team of them, to make those decisions on your behalf. The fund follows a stated investment objective, and the manager selects holdings that align with that goal.

For example, a fund that aims for long-term growth might hold primarily large-cap U.S. stocks. A fund focused on income might hold a mix of dividend-paying stocks and bonds. The fund’s prospectus, a document you can access before investing, spells out exactly what the fund is trying to do and how it prepares to do it.

Industry observers note that investors buy and sell mutual fund shares directly through the fund organization or through a brokerage account. You can invest a specific dollar amount rather than buying a whole number of shares, making them accessible to investors at just about any level.

There are thousands of mutual funds available, but most fall into a handful of broad categories.

These funds invest primarily in stocks. They can be further broken down by the size of the companies they hold (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap), the style of investing (growth vs. value), or the geography (U.S. only, international, or global). Stock funds carry more risk than bond funds but also offer greater long-term growth potential.

Bond funds (fixed income funds).

According to recent reports, bond funds hold debt securities issued by governments, corporations, or municipalities. They are generally considered less volatile than stock funds and are often used to add stability to a portfolio. However, they also tend to produce lower returns over long periods.

These funds hold a combination of stocks and bonds within a single fund. The allocation varies by fund, but the idea is to provide both growth and income while smoothing out some of the volatility of a pure stock fund.

According to recent reports, money market funds invest in short-term, low-risk debt instruments. They aim to maintain a stable value and are often used as a place to park cash. The returns are modest, and they are not a long-term wealth-building strategy.

Index funds are a specific type of mutual fund that tracks a market index, such as the S&P 500, rather than relying on active stock picking. Because they are passively managed, they tend to have much lower fees than other types of mutual funds. Over the long run, they have consistently outperformed most actively managed alternatives after costs are taken into account.

This distinction is one of the most key things to understand about mutual funds, and it directly affects your returns.

An actively managed fund employs a portfolio manager who researches investments, makes judgment calls, and trades frequently to outperform the market. This sounds appealing. Who would not want a professional trying to beat the market on their behalf?

In a recent development, the problem is that most actively managed funds do not beat the market over the long run, especially after fees are factored in. Study after study over multiple decades has shown that the majority of active fund managers underperform a simple index fund over a ten-year period. Yet they charge significantly more for the attempt.

A passively managed fund, like an index fund, does not try to beat the market. It simply tracks it. The holdings change only when the underlying index changes. Because no active management is required, the fees are a fraction of those charged by actively managed funds.

Recent findings suggest that for most long-term investors, a low-cost index fund is the better choice. The math is straightforward: lower fees mean more of your return stays in your pocket, and that difference compounds significantly over decades.

Sources indicate that fees are one of the most overlooked factors in investing, and they deserve your full attention. Here are the main ones to know.

Sources indicate that the expense ratio is the annual cost of owning a fund, expressed as a percentage of your investment. A fund with a 1.00% expense ratio costs you $10 per year for every $1,000 you have invested. That may sound small, but over 30 years of investing, that difference compared to a fund charging 0.05% can amount to tens of thousands of dollars.

Some mutual funds charge a sales commission, called a load, either when you buy (front-end load) or when you sell (back-end load). A front-end load of 5% means that only $950 of every $1,000 you invest actually goes into the fund. There is no reason to pay a sales load when thousands of excellent no-load funds are available.

Industry observers note that these are marketing and distribution fees charged by some funds. They are baked into the expense ratio and can add up. A fund with a high 12b-1 fee is often a sign that the fund is spending money on sales and marketing rather than managing your investment.

In a recent development, when you invest in a mutual fund, you immediately own a small piece of every asset the fund holds. A single investment gives you exposure to hundreds or even thousands of companies, which spreads your risk far more effectively than buying individual stocks ever could.

Sources indicate that for investors who do not want to research individual securities, mutual funds hand the decision-making over to professionals. This is especially relevant for bond funds and specialty funds, where the research involved is more complex than evaluating stocks.

According to recent reports, most mutual funds have low minimum investment requirements, and many allow you to invest in dollar amounts rather than whole shares. This makes them a practical option for investors who are just getting started or working with a limited budget.

According to recent reports, mutual funds in the United States are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Fund companies are required to disclose their holdings, fees, and performance data regularly. That transparency makes it relatively easy to compare options and know exactly what you are getting into.

Fees can erode your returns significantly.

Recent findings suggest that this is the biggest problem with many mutual funds, particularly actively managed ones. High expense ratios and sales loads reduce your effective return every single year. Over a long investing horizon, that drag is substantial. Always check the expense ratio before investing in any fund.

Because mutual funds are priced once daily at market close, you cannot buy or sell during trading hours at a live price. For long-term investors, this is rarely a concern. But it is worth understanding how mutual funds differ from ETFs in this regard.

When a mutual fund sells holdings at a profit, it distributes those capital gains to shareholders at the end of the year. Even if you did not sell any of your own shares, you may owe taxes on those distributions. This is less of an issue in tax-advantaged accounts like a 401(k) or IRA, but it is something to keep in mind for taxable brokerage accounts.

It is possible to hold too many mutual funds that overlap in their holdings, leaving you with a bloated, redundant portfolio. Owning five different large-cap U.S. stock funds does not give you five times the diversification. It mostly just gives you five sets of fees.

According to recent reports, with thousands of mutual funds available, narrowing down your options does not have to be complicated. A few straightforward criteria will get you most of the way there.

Mutual funds are among the most practical investments available to everyday investors. They make it easy to build a diversified portfolio without needing to research and manage individual securities. For most people, the primary vehicle for building wealth over time is a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account.

According to recent reports, that stated, not all mutual funds are worth your money. Actively managed funds and those with high sales loads or steep expense ratios consistently underperform lower-cost alternatives over the long run. The evidence strongly favors low-cost index funds as the core of most investors’ portfolios.

Recent findings suggest that the most key step is to start. Aim to invest at least 10% of your gross income consistently, keep your costs low, stay diversified, and give your money time to grow. The mechanics of which specific funds you choose matter far less than the discipline of contributing regularly over many years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, once you’re preapproved for a mortgage, hold off on newly introduced credit cards, car loans, store financing, and co-signing until after closing. Your lender checks your credit again just before you close, and one new monthly payment can push your debt payments over its limit. That can delay the closing or cancel the loan.

Lenders base your approval partly on your debt-to-income ratio, the share of your monthly income before taxes that goes to debt payments, figured from the debts you had when you applied. Under Fannie Mae’s rules for the loans it buys, lenders must recalculate that ratio whenever upcoming debt turns up, right up to closing day.

In that ratio, every card adds its minimum payment, store cards included. Even a small latest payment can push you past the limit if you were approved close to it, and over the limit, the loan no longer qualifies.

In a recent development, say a buyer earns $7,500 a month before taxes, her lender caps the ratio at 45%, and she’s approved at 43%. A week before closing, she opens a store card for $4,000 of furniture. Its $160 minimum payment lifts her ratio to 45.1%, and the closing slips two weeks while she pays off the card and the lender reviews the loan again.

Until you close, put these off:.

Recent findings suggest that paying every bill on time stays essential, since a late payment can show up when the lender checks your credit before closing. Comparing several mortgage lenders is still fine. Send every application within about two weeks, and credit scores count them as a single credit check.

Pick out the furniture now, then buy it after closing day with savings rather than a latest store card.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

What Are Target Date Funds?

📅 27 May 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1209 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In this article, we will break down what target date funds are, how they work, what they cost, and why a low-cost index fund strategy may serve most investors better in the long run.
  • A target-date fund is a type of mutual fund designed to serve as a single, all-in-one retirement investment.
  • The fund holds a mix of stocks and bonds, and that mix automatically shifts over time as your target date gets closer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this article, we will break down what target date funds are, how they work, what they cost, and why a low-cost index fund strategy may serve most investors better in the long run.

A target-date fund is a type of mutual fund designed to serve as a single, all-in-one retirement investment. You pick the fund that most closely matches the year you initiative to retire, and the fund handles everything else. If you plan to retire around 2050, for example, you would choose a fund labeled something like “2050 Retirement Fund” or “Target Date 2050.”.

The fund holds a mix of stocks and bonds, and that mix automatically shifts over time as your target date gets closer. Early on, the fund is weighted heavily toward growth stocks. As retirement approaches, the portfolio gradually shifts toward bonds and more conservative holdings to reduce risk.

The appeal is obvious. You make one decision, contribute regularly, and the fund adjusts itself. For people who want to set it and forget it, that sounds like a dream. But there is more to the story.

Target date funds are known as “fund of funds.” Rather than holding individual stocks or bonds directly, they hold a collection of other mutual funds, typically a mix of domestic stock, international stock, and bond funds.

The fund manager adjusts the allocation over time according to a schedule called a glide path. When you are decades away from retirement, the fund might hold 90% stocks and 10% bonds. As you get closer to your target year, that ratio shifts until the fund is much more conservative, sometimes holding more bonds than stocks by the time you retire.

The glide path is simply the schedule that determines how the fund’s asset allocation changes over time. Think of it as the fund’s long-term blueprint for gradually reducing risk.

Different fund providers use different glide paths, and this matters more than most people realize. Some funds are more aggressive early on and pull back dramatically as retirement nears. Others maintain a higher stock allocation even into and through retirement, which some financial planners argue is actually smarter given how long retirement can last.

The key thing to understand is that the glide path is not customized for you. It is a one-size-fits-all formula based on your expected retirement year, nothing more. Your actual risk tolerance, health, spending looks, and other income sources are not factored in at all.

Industry observers note that the biggest selling point is that target date funds require almost no ongoing attention. You pick one fund, contribute regularly, and walk away. For someone who has no interest in managing their investments, that convenience is genuinely valuable.

Sources indicate that because target date funds hold a mix of stock and bond funds, you get broad diversification across asset classes in a single investment. You are not putting all your money into a single sector or company.

Over time, a portfolio can drift away from its intended allocation as different assets grow at different rates. Target date funds handle this automatically, which is one less thing you have to manage yourself.

Target date funds are not without their drawbacks, and for many investors, those drawbacks are significant enough to look for a better option.

Because target date funds are funds of funds, they often carry two layers of fees: the expense ratio of the target date fund itself and the underlying expense ratios of the funds it holds. Even a seemingly small difference in fees can cost you tens of thousands of dollars over a long investing career. Low-cost index funds, by comparison, often charge a fraction of what target date funds do.

It has been revealed that the glide path in a target-date fund is designed for the average investor retiring in a given year. But your situation is not average. You might have a pension, a working spouse, rental income, or a much higher risk tolerance than the fund assumes. None of that is reflected in how the fund manages your money.

In a recent development, when you hand everything over to a target date fund, you give up control over your allocation. If the fund has a heavy position in international stocks or bonds that you would rather avoid, there is not much you can do about it while staying in the fund.

Variable quality across providers.

Recent findings suggest that not all target date funds are created equal. The same target year fund from two different providers can have very different allocations, fee structures, and underlying holdings. Without digging into the details, it is easy to end up in a fund that does not match your actual needs.

This is where the comparison gets important. A target date fund is actively managed in the sense that a team of people decides how to allocate and rebalance it over time. An index fund, on the other hand, simply tracks a market index like the S&P 500. There is no active management involved, which is exactly why the fees are so much lower.

Decades of research consistently show that most actively managed funds underperform their benchmark index after fees. Target date funds are not immune to this problem. When you account for layered costs, many target-date funds trail what you would earn by simply holding a low-cost index fund over the same period.

Industry observers note that A simple alternative that many investors use is called a three-fund portfolio: a U.S. total market index fund, an international index fund, and a bond index fund. You set your own allocation based on your age and risk tolerance, rebalance once a year, and pay minimal fees. It takes about 30 minutes a year to manage.

Industry observers note that this approach gives you the same diversification as a target-date fund, with far more control and significantly lower costs. And as a general rule, the more of your return you keep rather than paying in fees, the better off you will be over time.

Target date funds are not the right choice for every investor, but there are situations where they make sense.

Even in these cases, it is worth checking the expense ratio. If your plan offers a target-date fund with an expense ratio above 0.50%, consider whether there are lower-cost index fund options within the same plan.

Recent findings suggest that target date funds solve a real problem: they make it easy for people who do not want to think about investing to still participate in the market. That convenience has real value.

It has been revealed that but for investors who are willing to learn even a little bit about how to manage their own allocation, a portfolio of low-cost index funds will almost always be the better long-term choice. The fees are lower, the control is greater, and the returns tend to be better over time.

If you are currently in a target date fund, that is not necessarily a problem. But it is worth understanding what you are paying and whether a simpler, lower-cost approach might serve you better. Investing at least 10% of your gross income is the priority. Where exactly that money goes is the next question worth asking.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your guest count sets the size of the biggest wedding bills, since every name adds a meal, drinks, and a seat, and a longer list needs a bigger venue. Decide how many guests your budget can host before you book anything, then cut the list to that number with rules you apply to everyone.

Couples married in 2025 spent an average of $292 per guest, according to The Knot’s 2026 Real Weddings Study.

Industry observers note that not every dollar of that average goes away when you cut a name, since the photographer, the band, and your attire cost about the same at any size. But the venue, the biggest single bill at $12,900 on average, has to hold everyone, and catering averaged $80 a person.

So each table of eight you drop cuts $640 from the catering bill at that average, plus the table’s drinks, chairs, linens, and centerpiece. Cutting a first draft of 150 names to 110 removes five tables and $3,200 in catering alone, and can let you book a smaller, cheaper room.

Set your guest count before you tour venues or ask for catering quotes, since both depend on it. Take your wedding budget, subtract the costs that won’t change with the count, and divide the rest by what each guest adds in food, drinks, rentals, and invitations.

Then cut to that number with rules that apply to both sides of the family:.

Answer everyone who asks the same way, by saying you kept the wedding small to stay on budget. A small ceremony now and a bigger, casual party later let you celebrate with the people you cut for far less than a reception for everyone. An invitation that arrives weeks after everyone else’s reveals the guest they were a backup, so mail any second round soon after the first.

Cut the list to your number before any save-the-dates go out, since everyone who gets one expects an invitation.

  • Industry observers note that if your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives.
  • A health sharing blueprint (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance tech giant.
  • Sources indicate that tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives. Health sharing plans have moved from a faith-based niche into a mainstream budgeting conversation. But before you switch, it’s worth understanding exactly what you’re trading away, not just what you’re saving.

A health sharing blueprint (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance tech giant. There’s no insurance contract, and no company is legally on the hook to pay your claims.

Sources indicate that tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed. Michigan’s insurance regulator adds that HCSMs aren’t classified as insurance because they don’t assume risk and have no legal obligation to pay members’ costs.

Example: Zion HealthShare is a modern health sharing community that markets itself as a lower-cost alternative to ACA plans, with no provider networks and members paying an “Initial Unshareable Amount” (their version of a deductible) before larger bills become eligible for sharing.

Read our review of Zion HealthShare.

Recent findings suggest that traditional health insurance is a regulated contract, an ACA marketplace initiative, an employer plan, or a private major-medical policy. The insurer must pay covered claims, cover pre-existing conditions from day one, and include the ACA’s essential health benefits (preventive care, maternity, mental health, and more), a distinction healthinsurance.org explains in detail when comparing HCSMs with ACA-compliant coverage.

Solo Health is another option built for self-employed people. It’s a self-funded major medical health proposal with a nationwide PPO network, and it works differently from both health sharing and ACA Marketplace coverage. Eligibility is based on a short health questionnaire. Read our full Solo Health review.

Employer-sponsored family premiums averaged $26,993 in 2025, and many 2026 ACA marketplace prepares are seeing median premium hikes of 18–20% as subsidies shrink and medical costs climb. By comparison, health sharing contributions often run $150–$400 per person per month, roughly 30–50% less.

Recent findings suggest that but that gap exists because health sharing intends aren’t required to guarantee anything. Traditional insurers already deny 19–20% of claims on average (some carriers reportedly higher), so even “real” insurance isn’t friction-free, but at least it comes with legal appeal rights and state oversight. A health share’s review process is informal and ministry-specific, with no equivalent legal backstop if a bill gets rejected.

Recent findings suggest that it works best for generally healthy families who don’t qualify for meaningful ACA subsidies, are comfortable handling more paperwork and negotiating bills themselves, and want lower fixed monthly costs in exchange for taking on more risk. It’s a weaker fit for anyone managing a chronic condition, planning a pregnancy, or who needs the legal certainty of a regulated contract.

Health sharing can meaningfully lower your monthly healthcare costs, but the trade-off is real: you’re giving up the legal guarantee, essential-benefit mandates, and regulatory protection that come with traditional insurance. For a healthy family stretched thin by rising ACA premiums, it can be a reasonable bridge option. For anyone with ongoing medical needs, the savings usually aren’t worth the uncertainty.

In a recent development, is a health sharing proposal the same as a health insurance policy?No. It’s a voluntary cost-sharing arrangement, not a legally binding insurance contract.

Can I use a health sharing plan and still contribute to an HSA?Not based on the health share alone; you also need to be enrolled in a genuine HDHP to be HSA-eligible.

Will a health sharing plan cover a pre-existing condition?Usually only after a waiting period, which varies by organization, often 12 to 36 months.

Does the ACA’s individual mandate penalty apply if I only have a health share?No, the federal individual mandate penalty was eliminated starting in 2019, so this isn’t a factor either way.

How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

📅 13 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2432 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well.
  • And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.
  • As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well. Back in February 2025, the market put the perfect cap on a multi year climb before stepping onto the wild roller coaster we’re presently riding. Since then it has seen some of the steepest drops and recoveries in history, losing a full 20% of its value at the bottom while somehow managing to end up right back near the peak as I’m writing this.

And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.

As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.

Industry observers note that as I write this, we still don’t know the outcome of the worldwide tariff and trade battle that our unpredictable government has unleashed upon the world. But we’re already seeing the results: businesses are bracing for massive changes, currencies and interest rates are reacting, and regular investors like you and me are wondering what the future holds for our early retirement funds. Surveying my own group of friends, the reactions span the whole range of emotions from “this is a giant Nothingburger” to “we’re all totally screwed.”.

So what’s the real answer? To get closer to that, we should start with the most basic question of:.

A tariff is just a sales tax charged by our government on goods which are imported into the country. They are paid by whoever is doing the importing – meaning you if you order something like an e-bike directly from a company in China, or by companies like Amazon, Walmart, or Apple which import products from other countries by the shipload.

But in the end, the tariffs aren’t paid by China or Amazon or Apple. They are paid by you, the end consumer, because if their cost of goods increases, a retailer is of course going to raise their prices to continue to make a profit.

Tariffs also affect companies directly: if Home Depot wants to build a new store or Chevron needs a new oil rig, the tariffs on imported steel, copper, lumber and a million other components will raise the cost of these construction projects. And they raise the cost of housing, because most of the building materials in houses come from multiple countries as well.

On average, tariffs will result in higher prices for everything just like any other broad-based sales tax. And just like most other taxes, the overall effect is to slow the economy and reduce our spending power. On the positive side, all that tax money flows into the government’s pocket which could help fund the national budget and even reduce the deficit.

Of course, every government needs at least some tax revenue to function, so it makes sense to use some mix of sales, income and corporate taxes to get there. The most crucial part is that the levels need to be as low as possible while still keeping the country running well, and as fair and predictable as possible, so that people and businesses have an incentive to work hard and the ability to plan far into the future.

It has been revealed that and that’s where our current tariff regime gets it completely backwards. Donald Trump is throwing around random, extremely high tariff numbers as threats, then walking them back and changing them on an almost daily basis..

Whoa, that Sounds Mostly Bad – Is There a Good Side of Tariffs?

In a recent development, sometimes, a country will use tariffs to protect their own domestic industries. For example, if you put a tax on imported Hondas, then General Motors cars will gain a competitive advantage – so GM will make more money. In this example, most consumers end up losing due to increased prices and decreased selection. But at least domestic auto manufacturers and their employees are happy.

This can be strategic (for example we might want to slap a tax on imported fighter jets to make sure Boeing and Lockheed can remain in business, for national defense purposes.) Or it can be corrupt (a politician might receive funding from kingpins in the steel industry, and in return then push through tariffs on imported steel to protect the profits of US steelmakers.).

And this isn’t just a Trump or Republican thing either – Joe Biden used tariffs during his terms in an attempt to please swing-state voters. One of the worst examples was a tax on imported solar panel components (which Trump has since raised even further, proving that Boneheadedness can be Bipartisan). These are sheets of cheap glass that literally pump the cheapest energy and easiest wealth into your country for 30 years as soon as you plug them in. Cheap energy lowers everyone’s cost of living while also boosting industry. There is no good reason to block such wealth from flowing across your borders.

Can Tariffs Bring Us More Jobs?

Let’s go back to that hypothetical tax on Hondas, and let’s say it’s a massive one like $5000. At that level, many buyers will start heading over to the GM dealer next door to consider what he’s selling. Sure, the GM cars may not be as good, but for five grand some people are going to settle in order to save some money.

In a recent development, because of this, GM’s sales go up. So they hire more employees and build more factories. They might even develop some upcoming models and new technologies in response to all that new demand. More people learn advanced skills and in the best case it becomes a virtuous circle.

According to recent reports, but in exchange for this boom in the auto industry, everyone else has to pay more for slightly shittier cars and trucks. Higher vehicle prices means Amazon will have to spend more on their delivery fleet, so they will raise prices slightly on everything they sell. Somewhere a startup tech giant or a medical breakthrough will be just a bit less likely to happen, because they are operating in an environment that is just a bit more expensive and a bit less efficient.

On top of that, with GM liberated from the hassle of competing with Honda, it will have less incentive to innovate and streamline itself. So its overall trajectory will be slower and less efficient even if its profits are higher.

This significant picture effect is why most economists agree that tariffs should be used very sparingly. They almost always cause unexpected damage, decrease overall employment and slow down an economy, but sometimes (like for food security or national defense) those costs are worth paying.

So Why is Donald Trump Throwing Around Tariffs Like They Are The Best Thing Ever?

Sources indicate that this has been confusing to almost everyone. If you take him at his word, he appears to have a Bizarro Opposite Universe belief system about economics. Donald has claimed in speeches that the tariffs will somehow make us wealthier. He’s focusing on the first-order effects like GM hiring more workers, while completely ignoring the fact that everything else in the country gets less efficient in exchange.

Sources indicate that but when he announces larger tariffs, share prices go down, because everyone who actually runs or invests in US companies knows that of course they will make less money on average. When tariffs are paused or reduced, share prices go back up. Yet he keeps wielding the threats and we go back and forth.

It seems to be obvious to everyone except Donald himself that Tariffs are just a national sales tax rather than some clever sneaky strategic weapon, which leads to various theories that okay, maybe he knows that too but is just pretending in order to gain some influence.

The basic theory goes like this:.

It has been revealed that so right now our entire economy is subject to the whims of a single person.. And as long as this is the case, we’re just the same as any other dictatorship – something our constitution was supposed to prevent with the whole “three independent branches of government” thing.

But presidents have tried to break out of their constitutional cage and get more power many times in the past, and this is just the latest example. The real test will be if our system eventually manages to stop this abuse and put itself back in balance as it always has in the past. You can already see this fight beginning to play out in our court system, in this Economist article:.

How Substantial are the Tariffs Right Now?

According to recent reports, even without the 145% nonsense numbers that were thrown around a few months ago, they are still far higher than they have been in the last 75 years or more. While it would be hard to pin down the current numbers in a stationary blog post like this one, the key thing to remember is that our current US economy is built around very low tariffs and relatively free trade.

Why haven’t I noticed Prices Going Up Yet?

While the US economy is fueled by a constant stream of cargo ships, as a whole we function like the biggest cargo ship of all: we have a huge inventory and it takes a while to change directions.

It has been revealed that so in normal times, we already have several months of inventory of most things in the country. And then when all this drama started, importers started placing even more orders to stockpile things in advance before the tariffs hit. And now that they are in place, we’re importing a lot less stuff.

Recent findings suggest that for now, we’re still using up the stockpiled inventory, but imports have dropped significantly so we’re rapidly running out of cheap goods. If that happens, we will probably start seeing shortages and price increases throughout this summer or fall. For some things like plastic party trinkets, we can do just fine without. But if we lose access to core useful things like tools and machinery, the economic consequences will be much less fun.

The Dark Side and the Bright Side.

The most crucial phrase to remember in US politics and economics is the phrase “This too shall pass.” The only mystery right now is that we don’t know exactly how it will pass. So we could sketch out a few scenarios:.

1) The current crazy-high tariffs really do stick around:.

Recent findings suggest that I personally think this is the less likely scenario because nobody really wants it. But just as a thought experiment, it might go something like this:.

2) They do end up being just a negotiating tactic and we go back to mostly low tariffs.

In other words, the best way to win the tariff game is not to play it.

Just as much of US prosperity is built upon our huge population of 330 million people living in 50 states with open borders and no trade restrictions, all (friendly) countries of the world can benefit from the free exchange of goods, services and even people. We’re all human beings and if we treat each other with a collaborative respect, we all grow richer.

Epilogue: Is it Almost Over Already?

Recent findings suggest that I started writing this article on April 2nd, when Donald confirmed his “Liberation Day” and the stock market reacted with the biggest drop since 1932. Some people panicked and locked in big losses despite decades of warnings from your favorite financial bloggers, like this unfortunate soul in the comments to a JL Collins post:.

But as I watched over the next two months, we have bounced our way back up – with each drop in proposed tariffs triggering a corresponding increase in stock prices (a measure of investor enthusiasm of how bright our future looks).

In a recent development, right now, the US stock market is just about back to its all-time high. This doesn’t match with our current level of tariffs, which are still about seven times higher than they were before the circus opened. But it shows that investors believe it’s all going to end with a truce and a resumption of free-ish international trade.

Industry observers note that if they’re wrong, the roller coaster ride will still have some more fun in store for us. But as long as we eventually end our current experiment in “emergency” tariff dictatorship and get back to functioning as a democracy, things should be just fine in the long run. I’m still 100% invested myself, so that’s where I place my bet.

The Biggest Lesson: Don’t Form Your Opinions Based on News Headlines.

Recent findings suggest that decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us, with just a bit of sizzle and spice to pull in our attention. Unfortunately, nowadays the priorities have flipped where the primary goal is attention, and accuracy carries little or no weight. Even a totally inaccurate article makes money for the publisher.

So while Democrats and Republicans like to do battle over which media sources are biased, in reality they’re all wrong: all click-funded commercial media is biased – sometimes politically but even more importantly biased towards generating outrage and fear, because those generate more money.

There are two solutions to this:.

1) Either ignore the media completely and focus on your own life, or.

2) Become a subject matter expert on things you really care about, and then read the original sources whenever you want to learn about something.

I mostly practice option #1, but as a science and technology nerd I get into #2 in just the areas I find most interesting. And it’s amazing how the more deeply you understand a subject, the more you see just how wrong most media stories are about your area of expertise. Which means they’re probably pretty wrong about almost everything.

So as always, with this lesson learned it’s time to shut down that phone and laptop, exhale all our worries and get back outside with your real-life family and friends. See you in a few months!

  • Paid on time, a student loan helps your score most through payment history, which makes up 35% of a FICO score, and the years you carry it lengthen your credit history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every on-time student loan payment builds your credit, just as car loan payments do. A federal loan gives you 90 days before a late payment reaches your credit reports, where it stays for seven years. Set up autopay now, and if a payment gets hard to make, switch repayment plans before you miss one.

When missed federal student loan payments returned to credit reports in early 2025, more than 2.2 million newly delinquent borrowers saw their scores fall more than 100 points, the Federal Reserve Bank of Upcoming York found.

Paid on time, a student loan helps your score most through payment history, which makes up 35% of a FICO score, and the years you carry it lengthen your credit history. A significant balance isn’t scored like credit card debt near its limit. FICO compares what you still owe with what you borrowed, and paying it down counts in your favor.

According to recent reports, the servicer that bills a federal loan reports a missed payment to the credit bureaus once it’s 90 days late. Most federal loans default after 270 days without a payment, and the default goes on your reports too. Private lenders set their own rules, and some report a missed payment as soon as 30 days after it’s due.

Autopay makes each payment on time even if you forget, and the Education Department trims the rate for borrowers who use it. If the payment is too high, an income-driven blueprint sets it from your income and family size, and a deferment or forbearance temporarily pauses payments, though interest usually keeps building. Either one, set up before a payment is 90 days late, keeps it off your reports. After a default, rehabilitation, nine affordable monthly payments agreed with the loan’s holder, removes the default from your credit history but not the late payments before it.

According to recent reports, picture two graduates, each with $30,000 in federal loans and three months between jobs. One skips three payments, so by her fourth due date the first is about 90 days late and goes on her reports for seven years. The other calls her servicer first and switches to an income-driven blueprint based on what she earns, so she never misses one.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A cashless store is legal in most of the U.S., since federal law leaves it to each store whether to take cash.
  • The “legal tender for all debts, public and private” line on every bill reads like a rule that stores must take it.
  • Legal tender means cash is a valid way to pay a debt, the Federal Reserve explains, but no federal law requires a private business to take it for a purchase.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A cashless store is legal in most of the U.S., since federal law leaves it to each store whether to take cash. But 10 states, and cities such as Philadelphia and San Francisco, require most stores and restaurants to accept it. Check your state’s and city’s rules before you count on paying cash, and carry a backup card.

The “legal tender for all debts, public and private” line on every bill reads like a rule that stores must take it. It isn’t one.

Legal tender means cash is a valid way to pay a debt, the Federal Reserve explains, but no federal law requires a private business to take it for a purchase.

Industry observers note that in November 2026, the Pew Research Center counted 10 states that make most in-person businesses take cash: Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island, Colorado, Connecticut, Oregon, Delaware, Montana, New York, and Maryland. New York’s law took effect in March 2026 and Maryland’s in October, and Illinois’s starts in January 2028. Pew counted 10 cities and counties too, including Philadelphia, San Francisco, Detroit, Miami-Dade County, and Washington, D.C.

Before you insist on paying cash, know what your law leaves out. The laws mostly cover stores and restaurants, but Connecticut’s law exempts membership warehouse clubs such as Costco, Oregon’s exempts farmers markets and roadside stands, and Newly introduced York’s lets a store turn down bills over $20. Some, New York’s among them, also exempt a store with a kiosk that turns cash into a prepaid card, which in New York must be free to use.

If a store your law covers still refuses your cash, ask for a manager and mention the law. If that fails, report the store to the office that enforces it, such as New York’s attorney general.

Where no law applies, a card-only venue may offer one of those kiosks anyway. Say a stadium’s concession stands take only cards and its kiosk turns your $20 into a prepaid card. Look for a fee on its screen before you insert the bill, and use up the balance, since some prepaid cards charge a fee once they sit unused.

Keep a debit card from a free checking account, or a prepaid card with no monthly fee, in your wallet next to your cash, so you can still pay where cash isn’t taken.

Compare the best free checking accounts for a debit card with no monthly fee.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A significant party’s cost is mostly food and drink multiplied by your guest list, so set a per-guest budget before you invite anyone.
  • Thumbtack’s catering cost guide puts a caterer’s buffet at about $23 to $25 a guest, so feeding 40 people that way runs $920 to $1,000.
  • According to recent reports, timing is the cheapest fix, because guests who have just eaten want snacks, not a full plate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A significant party’s cost is mostly food and drink multiplied by your guest list, so set a per-guest budget before you invite anyone. Then start at 2 p.m. or 8 p.m., when guests have already eaten, and make it a potluck so each family brings a side.

Thumbtack’s catering cost guide puts a caterer’s buffet at about $23 to $25 a guest, so feeding 40 people that way runs $920 to $1,000.

According to recent reports, timing is the cheapest fix, because guests who have just eaten want snacks, not a full plate. Marquette University’s event planning tips say 6 to 8 appetizers a guest are enough at a late-afternoon or late-evening reception, against 10 over the lunch hour.

Then split the menu with your guests. A potluck sign-up that gives each family a kind of dish, such as salad, chips, fruit, or dessert, keeps you from getting five bowls of pasta salad. “Bring your own drinks” on the invitation covers the beer and wine.

Work from the per-guest number. A 2 p.m. graduation open house for 40 with a $250 budget has about $6 a guest to spend. Say pork shoulder is on sale for about $2.20 a pound. Twenty pounds costs about $45 and cooks down to roughly 10 pounds of meat, a quarter pound for each of 40 sandwiches. The rest of the list, from buns and lemonade to paper goods, a fruit tray, and a sheet cake, fits in the remaining $205, while families bring the sides.

Holiday hosts can save more by buying the Thanksgiving turkey from the grocery ads and spending Latest Year’s Eve at home rather than going out.

Send the invitation as one group text with the start time, a link to the sign-up sheet, and “bring your own drinks” on the last line.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that before you buy a rental or turn your home into one, add up every cost of owning it, from the mortgage and taxes to repairs, empty months, and management. Go ahead only if the rent covers them all with room to spare and you’re ready to screen tenants, follow landlord-tenant laws, and take repair calls.

Rent that beats the mortgage payment doesn’t make a rental profitable. The gap has to pay for everything else the property costs.

Say a couple rents out their old condo, and its mortgage payment, property taxes and insurance included, is $1,600 a month. At $1,900 in rent, they expect to clear $300 a month, or $3,600 a year. Then two empty months cost $3,800 in rent, and a new water heater and a cleaning between tenants cost $3,200. They end the year $3,400 behind.

Before you buy, or rent out the home you’re leaving, budget for four more costs:.

Depreciation lowers the tax on your rent because you deduct the building’s cost, though not the land’s, over 27.5 years. The IRS also lets owners who approve tenants and repairs deduct up to $25,000 a year of rental losses from other income, an allowance that shrinks to nothing at higher incomes. Any loss beyond it waits for a later year.

It has been revealed that A rental is also a job. Someone has to screen applicants, follow fair housing rules and your state’s security deposit and eviction laws, and take the midnight call about a leak. That’s you, or a manager you pay. A real estate fund gives you a stake in property without that work, so count your time as a cost too.

Become a landlord only if the rent still leaves money after every cost above, with repairs and management figured at the high end of their ranges.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A home workout plan needs no trainer or paid app. Federal exercise guidelines call for at least 150 minutes of brisk walking or other moderate cardio a week, plus strength work on two or more days. Put each session on your calendar, train with body weight and household items, and add reps or minutes every week or two.

The 150 minutes and the two strength days come from the Department of Health and Human Services’ Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans. They tell you how much exercise is enough, which is part of what a trainer or a paid app charges for.

Industry observers note that A walk counts as brisk at 2.5 miles per hour or faster, and 75 minutes of vigorous activity like running meets the cardio target on its own. For strength work, the guidelines say to do each move until one more repetition would be hard, and a single set of 8 to 12 repetitions per move is effective.

Recent findings suggest that five moves cover every major muscle group: squats and lunges for your legs and hips, push-ups for your chest, shoulders, and arms, rows for your back, and a plank for your core. Do push-ups against a kitchen counter until you can do 8 from the floor. For rows, bend forward and pull a gallon jug of water or a backpack loaded with books toward your ribs, and wear the backpack for squats once body-weight squats feel easy.

According to recent reports, for cardio, pick what you’ll keep doing, whether that’s brisk walks, runs, or a free workout video. Then give every session a day and a time, as you would an appointment. A 40-year-old could do 25-minute strength sessions on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday and 50-minute brisk walks on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday. That’s 150 minutes of cardio and three strength days, with Sunday off, at no cost.

According to recent reports, write down the repetitions for each move and the minutes of each cardio session, in a notebook, a free app, or the printable proposal from the federal Move Your Way activity planner. Every week or two, add two repetitions, a second set, more weight in the backpack, or five minutes of cardio, since the guidelines call for raising activity gradually over weeks to months.

If you’ve been inactive, start smaller, with 10-minute walks and one strength day a week, and build to the full plan over several weeks.

If fear keeps you from starting a business, make the worst case small enough to live with. Start on the side while you keep your job, and before you spend anything, set a budget you can afford to lose and a date to decide whether it’s working. Spend more only once customers are paying.

Plenty of owners already run a business alongside another job. Nearly four in five U.S. small businesses have no employees, a 2026 Federal Reserve report found, and for almost four in 10 of those, the business isn’t the main owner’s only job.

You don’t need a brand-latest idea either. A better or more local version of something people already buy is enough. A service you know how to do can start with a laptop, a simple website, and some software. On the side, it takes only the hours you give it. And if you sell under your own legal name, you don’t have to register the business anywhere, the Small Business Administration indicates, though you’ll still need any license or permit your work requires before your first sale.

Keeping your job also improves the business’s odds. In a study published in the Academy of Management Journal, people who started a business while still employed and went full time later were 33% less likely to fail than those who quit a job to start one.

Before you spend anything, set three limits:.

Sources indicate that picture a bookkeeper who caps her costs at $500 for software and a website, then does the books for three local shops on weekends. After a year, the clients pay enough that she cuts her job to part time.

Expect mistakes, like a price set too low or a client who pays late. On a small budget each one costs little, so fix it promptly instead of trying to prevent every one.

Write the three limits down today, before you buy anything for the business.

Link the bank account you pay them from to Experian Boost, a free tool that adds them to your Experian report. It’s most worth doing when your credit history is short or your score sits just under a lender’s cutoff.

These bills usually reach a credit report only when one goes unpaid and lands in collections, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau indicates.

Boost doesn’t wait for the phone manufacturer or utility to report. It reads two years of payments in the account you connect and lets you pick which qualifying bills go on your Experian report. Experian highlights you right away whether your FICO Score 8, one version of the FICO score, went up.

Only your Experian report gets those payments, so lenders checking your reports at the other two credit bureaus, Equifax and TransUnion, won’t see the gain. Experian also states not every lender uses a score that Boost affects, and most mortgage lenders don’t.

Recent findings suggest that payments by check or through apps like Venmo don’t count. Some rent paid online counts too, though Boost is just one of several ways to get rent reported. You also need enough history for a FICO Score, meaning at least one account active six months or more and one reported in the last six.

Recent findings suggest that take a renter with one credit card who links the account she pays her phone and electric bills from. Boost finds two years of on-time payments on both. Experian indicates people whose score rose gained 14 points on average. The trade-off is letting Experian see that account’s payment history. Some scores also stay flat or even drop. If hers drops, she can disconnect, and Experian says the score should return to where it was.

Connect your bill-paying account now, ahead of any credit application, and leave it linked so Experian keeps checking for latest on-time payments.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

Make Each Money Resolution a SMART Goal – Then Automate the First Step

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that rewrite each money resolution as a SMART goal, one that’s specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound, so “save more” turns into a dollar amount, a deadline, and a step you take every payday.
  • Sources indicate that neither “save more” nor “get out of debt” says how much, by when, or what to do this week.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that rewrite each money resolution as a SMART goal, one that’s specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound, so “save more” turns into a dollar amount, a deadline, and a step you take every payday. Automate that step, check your progress once a month, and shrink the target instead of quitting if you fall behind.

Sources indicate that neither “save more” nor “get out of debt” says how much, by when, or what to do this week. A resolution without those answers depends on motivation alone, and it stops when your motivation fades.

A SMART goal supplies all three. If you’re paid twice a month and start in January, “save more” becomes “move $250 to a high-yield savings account each payday until it holds $3,000 by June 30.” The account and the amount make it specific, and the balance makes it measurable. It’s achievable as long as $250 a paycheck fits your budget, relevant because $3,000 can pay for a car repair you’d otherwise put on a credit card, and time-bound by June 30.

Industry observers note that the other common money resolutions work the same way. At a 22% interest rate, “get out of debt” becomes “pay off my $2,400 card balance in 12 months by paying $225 a month and charging nothing upcoming.” “Spend less on takeout” becomes “keep restaurant and delivery spending to $200 a month, checked every Sunday.”.

Break each target into monthly steps, then automate the first one. Set up a recurring transfer to savings for the day after each payday, or a recurring card payment from checking, so the money moves even in a month you forget about the goal.

Recent findings suggest that then put a 10-minute check on your calendar for the same day each month to compare your progress with the plan. When a target proves too substantial, lower the amount or move the date instead of dropping the goal. A transfer cut to $150 a paycheck still adds up to at least $1,800 by June 30.

Work on one or two goals at a time, so each gets enough money and attention to make visible progress.

Write your first goal down today with its amount and its date, then schedule its first transfer or payment for the day after your next payday.

Industry News: How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2061 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon.
  • You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.
  • I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun new way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which mentioned something like,.

“Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”.

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:.

In a recent development, okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

It has been revealed that so I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect.

One of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:.

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:.

Sources indicate that but occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

In a recent development, I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

So Was This The Downfall of MMM?

According to recent reports, during the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Industry observers note that admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

In a recent development, then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

This is What “Fuck You Money” is For!

Sources indicate that it dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

Industry observers note that it reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

According to recent reports, experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning new things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

It has been revealed that one interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:.

It has been revealed that so I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

Industry observers note that so here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

Recent findings suggest that and of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well).

According to recent reports, but I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

Recent findings suggest that as with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:.

We will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that real estate wholesaling pays you a fee for putting a home under contract below market and selling the contract to an investor, so it’s a sales job.
  • The pitch, often from someone selling a course, promises a way into real estate without money or credit.
  • Sources indicate that you find them with mailers, lead lists, and calls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that real estate wholesaling pays you a fee for putting a home under contract below market and selling the contract to an investor, so it’s a sales job. Before you pay for a course, check whether your state requires a license or a disclosure to the seller, and add up what a few months of mailers would cost.

The pitch, often from someone selling a course, promises a way into real estate without money or credit. What the business takes is a marketing budget and a steady supply of owners who need to sell a rundown house fast.

Sources indicate that you find them with mailers, lead lists, and calls. When one agrees, you sign a purchase contract you can sell to another buyer, put down a small good-faith deposit called earnest money, and add an inspection contingency that lets you back out. Then you sell the contract to an investor for an assignment fee, or buy the house and resell it right away in what’s called a double closing.

Sources indicate that either way, you earn a fee for arranging a sale, not a return on property you hold, and it’s the gap between the seller’s price and the investor’s. The Oklahoma Real Estate Commission warns that many sellers don’t realize they’ve agreed to a wholesale deal, or how much the wholesaler makes on it.

Sources indicate that illinois requires a broker’s license once you wholesale twice within any 12 months, and Pennsylvania requires a license for every residential wholesale deal and gives the seller up to 30 days to cancel. Ohio and Connecticut require you and the seller to sign a disclosure before signing the purchase contract, and Oklahoma gives the seller two business days to cancel.

According to recent reports, say a latest wholesaler in Illinois spends $3,000 on mailers and lead lists over four months and closes one $8,000 assignment. She clears $5,000 before taxes, and she’d need a broker’s license to sell the second contract she’s working on.

It has been revealed that coaching can cost more than that profit. The Federal Trade Commission alleged that Zurixx used false promises of quick flipping and wholesaling profits to sell $1,997 seminars, then coaching that could run to tens of thousands of dollars. A 2022 settlement permanently banned the manufacturer and its owners from selling coaching.

Before your first mailer goes out, read your state real estate commission’s rules on wholesaling, and tell every seller in writing that you’re a wholesaler, not the final buyer.

Industry observers note that put your first energy-saving dollars into cheap fixes such as weatherstripping, LED bulbs, a programmable thermostat, and low-flow showerheads. They pay for themselves in about one to three years, while fresh windows can take decades. Check utility and state rebates before you buy anything.

According to recent reports, rank each upgrade by its payback, the years its savings take to cover its cost. Cheap fixes rank first because they cost little, even when a significant project saves more.

Energy Trust of Oregon, an efficiency nonprofit, puts the payback on cheap fixes at one to three years and on efficient new windows and solar panels at more than 10.

A 10-window vinyl replacement averaged $22,073 in the 2025 Cost vs. Value report, and Energy Star notes certified windows cut energy bills by up to 13% when they replace single-pane ones. Even on a $3,000 yearly energy bill, a 13% cut is $390 a year, so the job takes more than 55 years to pay back.

Start with a home energy audit from your utility, then work through the cheap fixes:.

It has been revealed that judge bigger projects the same way, using the price after rebates, and only if you’ll own the home longer than the payback. Energy Trust puts attic insulation at four to five years and a high-efficiency furnace, AC, or water heater at six to 10. Energy Star figures a certified heat pump water heater pays back its extra cost in about 2.7 years for a family of four replacing an electric tank. Federal tax credits for efficiency upgrades and solar ended for work done after 2025, but many utilities and some states still pay rebates. Energy Star’s Rebate Finder lists offers by ZIP code.

A project that adds to your home, rather than replacing something, can raise its assessed value. You can appeal a higher assessment yourself or through Ownwell, which charges only when your tax bill comes down.

Do the sealing and insulating first, since Energy Star says better insulation may let you choose a smaller, less expensive heat pump.
