College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That said, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like new credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most crucial issues for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Recent findings suggest that generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

One step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you proposal to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

It has been revealed that in fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Industry observers note that your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That said, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Recent findings suggest that some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit swiftly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

According to recent reports, while secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”.

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

In fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

According to recent reports, there are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

In a recent development, of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an issue with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

College students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Industry observers note that either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

Budget by Paycheck, Not by the Month – Give Each Bill a Payday

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (496 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re paid weekly or every other week, a monthly budget can balance on paper and still leave you short the week rent is due.
  • Industry observers note that say you take home $1,600 every other Friday and your $1,200 rent is due on the 1st.
  • In a recent development, budgeting by paycheck gives every bill, savings transfer, and spending allowance a specific payday, so each pay period has its own blueprint and its own leftover.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re paid weekly or every other week, a monthly budget can balance on paper and still leave you short the week rent is due. Budget by paycheck instead. Put every payday and due date on one calendar, then assign each bill to the check that arrives before it’s due.

Industry observers note that say you take home $1,600 every other Friday and your $1,200 rent is due on the 1st. The month’s two checks bring in $3,200, but if the rent comes out of the check that lands just before the 1st, that check has $400 left for two weeks of groceries, gas, and other bills.

In a recent development, budgeting by paycheck gives every bill, savings transfer, and spending allowance a specific payday, so each pay period has its own blueprint and its own leftover. In the example, setting aside $600 from each of the two checks before the 1st covers the rent and leaves each check $1,000.

Start with one calendar, on paper or in an app, that holds every payday and due date for the next three months. Include annual and quarterly bills, and divide each by the number of checks left before it’s due. A $720 car insurance bill due 12 checks from now takes $60 from each.

It has been revealed that then spread any bill too major for one check, like the rent, across the checks before it. Give savings transfers a payday too, and split groceries, gas, and fun money evenly across checks. When one check still carries too much, move a due date to the other half of the month. If your pay changes from check to check, start from a budget built on your worst month.

Recent findings suggest that plan each month’s bills on two checks, or four if you’re paid weekly. In most years, getting paid every two weeks means 26 checks, so two months bring a third, and weekly pay means 52, so four months bring a fifth. That extra check carries none of the monthly bills, so what it would have set aside for them, like the $600 for rent, is left over. Move it to savings, put it toward debt, or use it to get a month ahead on your bills.

Fill in the calendar before your next payday, and start with your biggest bill, usually rent or the mortgage.

  • Buying your home or renters insurance and your car insurance from one company usually earns a discount, but the bundle can still cost more than two separate policies.
  • It has been revealed that that happens because the discount comes off one company’s own prices.
  • In a recent development, some companies that sell both home and car insurance take 5% to 15% off your premium for two or more policies, the institute claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buying your home or renters insurance and your car insurance from one company usually earns a discount, but the bundle can still cost more than two separate policies. Before you switch or renew, get the bundled price and the best separate quotes for the same coverage, and buy whichever total is lower.

It has been revealed that that happens because the discount comes off one company’s own prices. The Insurance Information Institute says homeowners insurance for the same house can cost hundreds of dollars more at one insurer than at another.

In a recent development, some companies that sell both home and car insurance take 5% to 15% off your premium for two or more policies, the institute claims. It also tells buyers to make sure the bundle costs less than buying each policy from a different organization.

Sources indicate that say a family asks three insurers to quote the same coverage. The best bundle comes to $3,100 a year, and the cheapest home and car policies from two different companies total $2,850, so buying separately saves $250 a year. Next door, the best bundle costs $600 less than the cheapest separate policies, so the neighbors bundle.

According to recent reports, home, condo, and renters policies usually count toward the discount alongside a car policy. Some insurers also count a life insurance policy or an umbrella policy, which adds liability coverage on top of your home and car policies. Bundling also means one organization to call when a storm damages your roof and your car, and some insurers then charge one deductible instead of two. Treat those perks as a tiebreaker when the totals are close.

Separate quotes matter most when your car or your home is hard to insure. A driver with recent speeding tickets may find the lowest car rate at one tech giant and the lowest home rate at another. A home insured through your state’s FAIR strategy, the last-resort insurer for homes that private companies won’t cover, can’t be bundled at all, since the plan doesn’t sell car insurance.

Recent findings suggest that get every quote for the same coverage amounts, deductibles, and add-ons, from an agent or an online comparison tool. A quote with lower coverage amounts can look cheaper only because it pays less after a loss.

Before you split a bundle, ask your current insurer what the policy you’d keep will cost on its own, since dropping the other policy can end its discount.

Break a Costly Money Habit – Keep the Reward, Swap in a Cheaper Routine

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A costly money habit, like ordering delivery after a rough workday, starts with a cue and ends with a reward you want again.
  • Promising to stop leaves the cue and the reward in place.
  • The reward is often not the thing you buy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A costly money habit, like ordering delivery after a rough workday, starts with a cue and ends with a reward you want again. Work out what sets yours off and what it gives you, then strategy a cheaper routine that gives a similar reward, and mark each day you follow it.

Promising to stop leaves the cue and the reward in place. Each time the cue demonstrates up, you still want the reward, and you have to talk yourself out of it again.

The reward is often not the thing you buy. Delivery after a rough day gives you a night off from cooking and some comfort. Late-night browsing on shopping sites gives you a distraction, and a lottery ticket gives you a few days of daydreaming about a win.

A cheaper routine can give you that comfort, distraction, or daydream, so you still get what you were after.

In a recent development, track the habit for a week or two. Each time, note when and where it happens, how you feel, and what you get out of it. The time, place, or mood that keeps coming up is the cue, and the feeling it leaves you with is the reward.

It has been revealed that then set up a swap, a cheaper routine with a similar reward, before the cue comes back. Say two rough workdays a week end in a $30 delivery order, and a frozen dinner costs $7. Keep two in the freezer for those nights and call a friend on the walk home for the comfort. The dinner is plainer than takeout but still spares you the cooking. Those nights now cost about $60 a month instead of $260, a saving of about $200.

Take on one habit at a time. Mark each day you choose the swap on a calendar, and move what it saves into savings each week so you can watch the balance grow. A financial therapist can help with a habit that keeps returning despite a good swap.

Recent findings suggest that give the fresh routine time. In a University College London study, a new daily habit took 66 days on average to become automatic. Missing a single day had no lasting effect, but about half the volunteers didn’t do it often enough to form the habit. After a slip, run the swap again the next time the cue reveals up.

I recently completed three of the top Christian financial education programs for churches: SeedTime’s True Financial Freedom, Dave Ramsey’s Financial Peace University, and Crown Financial’s MoneyLife.

Sources indicate that these popular programs all claim to help you get control of your finances from a biblical perspective. However, they go about it in different ways with varying teaching styles and philosophies.

In this post, I’ll provide an in-depth look at each program – breaking down the unique features, strengths, weaknesses, and what’s actually included when you buy in.

It has been revealed that my goal is to give you the real deal on these courses so you can determine which one (if any) is the best fit for transforming your financial life in a way that aligns with your faith. Whether you’re deep in debt, building wealth, or simply trying to honor God with your money, this comparison will help guide your journey.

Let’s dive into the nitty-gritty details of each program:.

When it comes to pricing, Financial Peace University from Dave Ramsey sits in the middle. For an individual membership, it’s $69.99. They also offer bulk pricing for churches starting at around $800 for 10 memberships.

On the higher end, Seedtime’s True Financial Freedom charges $149 for an individual/couple license with regular deals making it available as low as $74. But they have some solid deals for Churches – you can get a bulk student license for as low as $48 per person if you buy multiple licenses. Or there’s an annual church subscription starting as low as $750 per year based on average attendance.

The most affordable option is Crown Financial’s MoneyLife course at just $29.95 for an individual purchase. I couldn’t find any publicly listed bulk pricing for churches, but being a non-profit, I’d expect them to be the cheapest route for congregations.

But as you’ll see, there are plenty more differences beyond just the price tags when comparing what’s actually included in each program.

True Financial Freedom, created by Bob Lotich and his wife Linda from SeedTime, is a financial literacy video course designed for churches that strikes a beautiful balance between biblical wisdom and practical money management strategies. The program’s goal is to equip Christians with the tools and mindset they need to experience true financial freedom while making an eternal impact for God’s Kingdom.

One of the standout features of True Financial Freedom is the engaging and relatable teaching style of Bob and Linda. They share their own financial struggles and triumphs with humor, transparency, and grace, making participants feel like they’re learning from wise, caring friends rather than aloof experts. This approach creates a safe, non-judgmental environment where participants can openly discuss their financial challenges and celebrate their progress.

Sources indicate that the program offers several unique benefits, such as the “Never 100” rule (their ‘done-is-better-than-perfect’ approach to adjust spending) and the “Straight A” strategy for automating finances. These concepts are not only memorable but also highly actionable in helping participants take control of their money and build lasting wealth.

Another strength of True Financial Freedom is its emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy. Through interactive workshops, participants are guided in developing a custom blueprint that fits their unique situation, goals, and values. This approach recognizes that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to personal finance and empowers participants to take ownership of their financial journey.

Recent findings suggest that true Financial Freedom is perfect for Christians who want to learn how to thrive financially while staying grounded in the Bible. The program teaches participants how to avoid the extremes of being “so heavenly-minded they’re no earthly good” or becoming so focused on building worldly wealth that they lose sight of what truly matters.

With its grace-filled approach and practical tools, True Financial Freedom helps Christians find the balance needed to change their financial life and make a lasting difference in the world in the process.

Financial Peace University, created by Dave Ramsey and his team at Ramsey Solutions, is a highly popular financial education program that has helped countless individuals and families get out of debt and build wealth. The program’s primary goal is to guide participants through a proven, step-by-step approach to taking control of their money and achieving financial peace.

In a recent development, dave Ramsey, the face of Financial Peace University, is known for his high-energy, tough love teaching style. He delivers hard-hitting truths about money with a sense of urgency and conviction that inspires participants to take action. However, some may find his approach a bit intense or even abrasive at times, likening it to going through bootcamp. While this style resonates with some, it may not be everyone’s preferred learning environment.

It has been revealed that the cornerstone of Financial Peace University is the “Baby Steps” system, a clear, prescriptive strategy for getting out of debt and building wealth. The program heavily emphasizes the debt snowball method, which involves paying off debts from smallest to largest, regardless of interest rates. This approach has proven highly effective in keeping participants motivated and helping them experience quick wins on their debt-free journey.

Recent findings suggest that while Financial Peace University does incorporate some biblical principles, its overall approach is more secular in nature. The program focuses primarily on the practical nuts and bolts of money management, with less emphasis on exploring the deeper spiritual implications of financial stewardship.

According to recent reports, financial Peace University is best suited for individuals and families who are drowning in debt and need a clear, actionable plan to get back on track. The program’s structured approach and intense motivation can be a lifeline for those feeling overwhelmed by their financial situation. However, those seeking a more personalized, grace-filled approach that deeply integrates biblical wisdom may find other programs more appealing.

MoneyLife, offered by Crown Financial, is a financial education program that takes a deeply biblical approach to money management. The program’s primary goal is to guide Christians in understanding and applying God’s financial principles to their lives, emphasizing the importance of seeing God as the ultimate provider and owner of all resources.

It has been revealed that one of MoneyLife’s distinguishing features is its strong focus on biblical teachings and spiritual practices related to money. The program dives deep into exploring how our financial decisions can reflect our faith and values, encouraging participants to align their money management with biblical principles. This emphasis on the spiritual aspects of finance sets MoneyLife apart from other programs that may focus more heavily on practical strategies.

The teaching style in MoneyLife tends to be more academic and classroom-like compared to other programs. Participants can expect a significant amount of reading materials and written assessments throughout the course. While this approach may appeal to those who prefer a studious learning environment, it may not be as engaging for individuals who thrive on interactive, video-based content.

It has been revealed that moneyLife offers some unique elements, such as personality assessments that help participants understand how their natural tendencies impact their financial decisions. The program is well-suited for those who want to explore the spiritual foundations of financial stewardship and align their money habits with their faith. Freelance Writing Rates – Quote by the Hours a Piece Takes, Not the Word Count

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that base every freelance writing quote on all the hours the piece takes, including research, interviews, and revisions.
  • A per-word offer can sound fair and still pay badly, because the word count claims nothing about the hours the piece takes.
  • Sources indicate that say a 1,500-word article takes you 6 hours to research, write, and revise, and you need to earn $75 an hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that base every freelance writing quote on all the hours the piece takes, including research, interviews, and revisions. Time a few typical pieces from start to finish, multiply the hours by the hourly rate you need, and quote the total as a project fee. Charge more for specialist topics, rush deadlines, and contracts that buy all rights.

A per-word offer can sound fair and still pay badly, because the word count claims nothing about the hours the piece takes.

Sources indicate that say a 1,500-word article takes you 6 hours to research, write, and revise, and you need to earn $75 an hour. Quote at least $450, which works out to 30 cents a word. A client offering 10 cents a word would pay $150 for the same 6 hours, or $25 an hour.

Thirty cents a word is in line with the Editorial Freelancers Association’s 2026 rate chart, built from a survey of more than 1,100 editorial freelancers. Its median range for work-for-hire articles and essays, which the client owns outright, runs from 25 to 45 cents a word.

Start from the hourly rate you need, which is the yearly income you want plus your business costs and self-employment tax, divided by the hours you can bill clients for. Then time three typical pieces from first research to final revision, including interviews, client calls, and email. Multiply your average hours by that rate, and quote the result as a flat project fee. For a client who pays by the word, divide the fee by the word count to get the per-word rate to ask for.

It has been revealed that specialist knowledge, technical or regulated subjects like medicine, credentials such as a CPA license, and rush deadlines all justify a higher fee. In the same rate chart, median ranges for work-for-hire medical and technical writing start at $1 a word. Selling more rights should cost the client more. A contract that buys all rights, or makes the piece work for hire, leaves you nothing to resell or reprint, so price it above one that buys only the right to publish the piece first.

Over time, collect testimonials, quote each new client above the last, and win more clients directly, since no platform takes a share of what they pay.

Divide every offer by the hours the piece will take, and counter any that fall short of your hourly rate with your project fee.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, most billionaires got rich by founding or holding a massive stake in a company that kept growing, not by earning a salary. You can use the same method on a small scale. Own stock through low-cost index funds and hold it for decades, and keep as much ownership as you can in any business you start.

Even a $1 million salary, saved in full, would take 1,000 years to add up to $1 billion.

According to recent reports, A stake in a tech giant is different, because its value rises as long as the company grows and you hold on. Jeff Bezos founded Amazon in 1994 and still owns 8% of it, the largest part of his fortune. Elon Musk’s fortune is mostly the 38% of SpaceX he owns, counting options to buy shares, with less in his nearly 11% of Tesla.

Forbes counts 71% of the 2026 Forbes 400, its list of the richest Americans, as self-made, meaning they built their fortunes rather than inheriting them. The rest started with an inheritance, like Alice Walton, whose fortune comes from her stake in Walmart, the company her father cofounded.

The part you can copy is ownership. If you start a business, keep as much of it as you can, because each share you sell early gives its future gains to the buyer.

Don’t copy how much of their wealth they keep in one company, though, since few single stocks pay off like that. Finance professor Hendrik Bessembinder found that four of every seven U.S. stocks since 1926 returned less over their lifetimes than one-month Treasury bills, which are short-term U.S. government debt. The best-performing 4% of companies produced the stock market’s entire net gain over that span.

A broad, low-cost index fund, such as one tracking the whole U.S. stock market, owns thousands of companies, so it holds the few massive winners without you having to pick them. At an assumed 7% average annual return, $10,000 left in one for 30 years grows to about $76,000, because each year’s gain earns returns too. Building wealth on an ordinary income works the same way, by spending less than you earn and investing the gap for decades.

Start investing in stocks with one such fund this month, since in that example the last 10 years add about $37,000, more than the roughly $29,000 the first 20 add.

Pick the broker that will hold that fund from the best online stock brokers for beginners.

Latest Update: My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

📅 16 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.
  • Industry observers note that but man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here.
  • I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

Industry observers note that but man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

But a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,.

“But I’m still gonna keep fighting it!”.

Recent findings suggest that yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

One of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder. And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health firm that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

In a recent development, long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

Sources indicate that another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

So I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s new firm, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:.

According to recent reports, the next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

And wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

In a recent development, it’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

This is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

Recent findings suggest that it turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

In many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

In a recent development, but there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

Many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

While this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me).

Recent findings suggest that distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

And while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

So I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty swiftly in the past.

But on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”.

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Recent findings suggest that many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”.

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

Since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a new, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term intends again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

So Why Doesn’t Everyone Do This?

Sources indicate that when you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that notes, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the glitch, you’ll see this:.

Stuff you should do BEFORE trying TRT:.

The modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

Since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

Recent findings suggest that many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

More modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

My hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

And it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower.

The great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The company that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

It has been revealed that note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

In a recent development, I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that paying off a non-medical collection helps only newer credit scores.
  • Sources indicate that on its own, paying won’t take a collection off your reports.
  • It has been revealed that FICO states its Score 9 and Score 10 ignore a collection agency’s account once it’s reported paid in full or settled to a zero balance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that paying off a non-medical collection helps only newer credit scores. FICO Score 9 and 10 and VantageScore 3.0 and 4.0 stop counting a collection once it’s paid, while paying does nothing for FICO Score 8 and older versions. Before you pay anything, get the collector’s terms in writing, including whether it will delete the account from your credit reports.

Sources indicate that on its own, paying won’t take a collection off your reports. It stays seven years from the missed payment that started it, paid or not, unless it’s a medical collection, which the credit bureaus drop once it’s paid.

It has been revealed that FICO states its Score 9 and Score 10 ignore a collection agency’s account once it’s reported paid in full or settled to a zero balance. VantageScore’s models have ignored paid collections since version 3.0 in 2013. Paying does nothing for FICO Score 8 or older versions.

That difference matters for a mortgage. The Federal Housing Finance Agency lets lenders selling loans to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac choose Classic FICO, an older model that still counts a paid collection, or VantageScore 4.0, which ignores it. Ask your lender which one it uses, and whether the loan requires collections paid off by closing.

Handle the collector in this order.

Say a collector agrees in writing to settle your $900 cable bill for $500. FICO Score 9 then treats the zero-balance account as paid and stops counting it, but the report lists it as settled, not paid in full. The $400 forgiven counts as taxable income unless an exception such as insolvency applies, with or without a Form 1099-C reporting it.

Pull your free weekly reports at AnnualCreditReport.com after you pay, and dispute the account with any bureau whose report doesn’t match the signed letter, sending a copy as proof.

#56713. Latest Update: The Hidden Benefit Of Being Retired In A Bear Market

Latest Update: The Hidden Benefit Of Being Retired In A Bear Market

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As my public equity portfolio gets obliterated thanks to being overweight tech stocks, I started dusting off my resume to go back to flipping burgers at McDonald’s.
  • Recent findings suggest that as every long-time investor knows, the name of the game is survival.
  • We're not in an official bear market, yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As my public equity portfolio gets obliterated thanks to being overweight tech stocks, I started dusting off my resume to go back to flipping burgers at McDonald’s. Then halfway through the application, I wiped away my tears and took a deep breath.

Recent findings suggest that as every long-time investor knows, the name of the game is survival. If you can make it through the downturn, good things usually await on the other side.

We're not in an official bear market, yet. But plenty of individual tech names have already fallen by over 20%, and when you're overweight those names, the index's official status doesn't matter much.

Industry observers note that so I thought it might be helpful for those who are retired, or who are close, to discuss the positives of going through a downturn. We'll also review how long downturns usually last so we can better prepare.

Industry observers note that as the midterm elections showed, a lot of people are not happy with the way our country has been led. But the discontent didn't appear overnight. The stock market was simply acting as a giant dose of Lidocaine.

As long as stocks kept going up, we could more easily bear higher oil prices, higher food prices, higher housing costs, higher college tuition costs, and explosive medical costs. After all, our investment returns were growing faster than inflation. $6 for a gallon of gas stings a lot less when your brokerage account is up $50,000 for the year.

In a recent development, but that tolerance for rising costs disappears the moment our investments start losing money. Suddenly, $89 a pound for wagyu feels personal.

When the wealth effect vanishes, consumers cut back. Fewer dinners out. Fewer vacations. The fresh car gets pushed out another year. With declining corporate profitability, companies accelerate layoffs to protect margins. The newly unemployed tighten spending even further.

Rinse and repeat until economists officially declare a recession six months after everybody already felt it.

It has been revealed that if you see the writing on the wall, you want want to get ahead of the layoffs by negotiating your own severance package. If you do, you will probably have an easier time getting a much better exit offer than being lumped with the masses.

Sources indicate that if you're newly retired, your biggest fear is sequence of returns risk. That's the risk of suffering major losses early in retirement while you're also withdrawing money to live on. Do that for too long and your portfolio may never recover.

It has been revealed that lose enough and you get forced back to work. Nobody who has tasted freedom wants to return to Monday morning status meetings and performance reviews from someone half their age.

Retirees who live off their investments should feel worse about a bear market more than the average worker. We don’t have a paycheck to cushion the blow. We may not have much spare cash flow to buy the dip either.

According to recent reports, but here's the key point. If your investments can survive the correction or bear market, you should actually feel good during a downturn. Not ecstatic, but relatively good. Because the alternative is working hard for no financial reward.

How do you know if you can survive? Run through this quick checklist:.

So how long will the pain last? History offers some comfort, provided you have the patience of a parent waiting for a toddler to put on his shoes while already 15 minutes late.

In a recent development, according to Capital Group, the S&P 500 has dropped 10% or more about once every 18 months since 1954. A 20%+ bear market highlights up about once every six years.

Industry observers note that in other words, if you plan on a 40-year retirement, expect roughly 25 corrections and six or seven bear markets. Declines are the price of admission, not a sign the world is ending. Get used to them.

Source: Capital Group, S&P 500 data from 1954 through 2025.

Sources indicate that hartford Funds, using Ned Davis Research data going back to 1928, counts 27 bear markets. Stocks fell 35% on average and took 289 days, or about 9.6 months, to hit bottom.

Bear markets were far more common during the Depression era. Since 1945, there have been 15, or one about every 5.1 years.

Recent findings suggest that two caveats before you get too comfortable. First, these figures measure peak to trough. Getting back to your old high takes longer. Second, the 1973 and 1980 bear markets each dragged on for more than 600 days. Averages are nice until you're living through the outlier.

Recent findings suggest that but here's the part that should make everyone feel better. Every S&P 500 correction since 1929 has been followed by a recovery, and the average return in the first year after the bottom was 52%. And the recoveries are happening quicker now, if we include the 2025 Liberation Day and 2026 Iran War events.

Recent findings suggest that hartford also found that about 42% of the S&P 500's strongest days over the past 20 years occurred during bear markets. Sell in a panic and you'll likely miss the rebound.

Industry observers note that my takeaway: In a realistic worst-case scenario, strategy on gutting out roughly 12 to 18 months of pain from peak to trough, with a longer tail to fully recover. That's why the one to two years of cash is fine, especially with interest rates still high.

The existential dilemma of a bear market is this:.

The correct answer is to work less hard and YOLO more. Let me explain using a concept I call Return On Effort (ROE).

Industry observers note that during a bull market, working less hard actually increases your Return On Effort because your investments provide most of the returns. Unless you have a sales job or some other role tightly correlated to performance, an extra 15 hours a week rarely moves the needle. You're better off riding the organization's growth.

During a bear market, working hard to run in place or lose money makes even less sense. There's nothing you can do to stem declining consumer confidence, new socialist policies, higher taxes, and so forth. Your boss isn't handing out raises while revenue is falling. See Google's collapse after having such a huge lead in the AI race.

Recent findings suggest that if anything, your extra effort earns you the privilege of doing the work of three colleagues who just got laid off. Congratulations on your 0% raise.

So you work less hard to protect your declining Return On Effort. Not because you're lazy. Because you're rational.

With this logic in mind, who works the least? The unemployed, the traditional retiree, and the early retiree.

Therefore, so long as your investments can withstand the beating, you're going to be just fine. Psychologically, as a retiree, you must push yourself to do less and have more fun.

In a recent development, happiness is relative. During a bull market, plenty of early retirees feel a twinge of FOMO watching former colleagues get promoted and cash fat RSU checks. During a bear market, that FOMO flips. Nobody envies the guy grinding through a reorg while his stock comp gets cut in half.

Whether you’re retired or still grinding away, a downturn offers some real perks.

1) Things get cheaper. When demand falls, so do prices for travel, hotels, and eventually real estate. Retirees with flexible schedules can travel off-peak and score deals that working parents can only dream about. Workers looking to buy their first home may finally face less competition.

2) You get to shop the sale. Retirees with passive income and a cash buffer get to buy when others are forced to sell. Workers get an even steadier advantage. Every paycheck and 401(k) contribution now picks up more shares at lower prices. Steady income plus a long time horizon makes you the natural buyer in a bear market.

It has been revealed that 3) Your kids get to buy the dip. I’ve written about how to use stock market downturns to make your kids millionaires. As a father, this is my favorite benefit of a bear market. Because the equity train finally stops long enough for kids to catch up and hop on board. A child has 50+ years of compounding ahead. A 30% drop today is a rounding error by the time they’re in their 50s.

Industry observers note that 4) Tax moves get better. Tax-loss harvesting offsets future gains. Roth conversions at depressed valuations mean you pay less tax on the same number of shares, and all the recovery happens tax-free.

Sources indicate that 5) The AI hedge is doing its job. Public AI stocks have gotten crunched. But there’s a flip side. If AI companies are struggling to justify their valuations, AI probably isn’t wiping out white-collar work as fast as everyone feared. That’s comforting for our kids, and for every worker wondering if their job will exist in 10 years.

6) You get humbled and build resilience. Being heavily overweight tech felt brilliant for years. Bear markets remind us we’re not as smart as we thought. My advice after every huge win is to go scrub all your toilets. Every downturn you survive makes you a calmer, better investor for the next one. If you’re still working, just make sure your emergency fund is solid, because layoffs tend to show up at the worst time.

You can’t control tech volatility, interest rates, or who wins elections. But you can control how you spend your time during a downturn.

Recent findings suggest that the market will eventually recover. It always has. When it does, the people who grinded through the downturn will be exhausted. Those of us who leaned into family, friends, and fitness will be well rested. Both groups will survive, which is what matters most.

If you’ve been thinking about retiring, a bear market may be the best time to pull the trigger. It means that in spite of the carnage, your finances are strong enough for you to break free. Waiting for the next bull market can feel safer, but it’s backwards.

Recent findings suggest that if your finances can support retirement while stocks are down 20% or more, your plan has already passed the stress test. You’re not retiring on inflated numbers that could vanish in the next correction. And since bear markets don’t last forever, a recovery may carry your retirement forward with a tailwind instead of a headwind.

In a recent development, compare that to the person who retires at the peak of a bull market, only to watch their portfolio drop 30% in the first two years. That’s sequence of returns risk at its worst.

So go play in the park. Take your kids to the beach. A downturn is the best time to enjoy the freedom you worked so hard to build, and maybe the best time to claim it.

Industry observers note that are you finding it more comforting to be retired during a downturn, or more stressful? How much of your portfolio would need to fall before you'd seriously consider going back to work? Do you agree that working less hard in a bear market is the rational move, or is that just a cop-out for the lazy? And for those still working, has the market selloff made you rethink how hard you're grinding? Are you using the downturn to fund your kids' investment accounts?

It has been revealed that if you want a roadmap for getting through downturns and coming out richer, pick up a copy of Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures, a USA Today bestseller. It covers how to keep investing when everybody else is scared, so you can reach financial independence sooner.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the 2025 tax law that made opportunity zones permanent set those terms, and they start on Jan.
  • In a recent development, after you sell stock, a business, or property at a gain, you have 180 days to put that gain into a qualified opportunity fund, which invests in designated low-income areas called opportunity zones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, put a capital gain into an opportunity zone fund only if you’d reinvest that money anyway and can leave it there for 10 years. For money invested from 2027, the tax on the gain is put off for five years and trimmed, not erased. The fund’s own growth goes tax-free only after a decade.

Recent findings suggest that the 2025 tax law that made opportunity zones permanent set those terms, and they start on Jan. 1, 2027, when the Treasury’s latest zones take effect.

In a recent development, after you sell stock, a business, or property at a gain, you have 180 days to put that gain into a qualified opportunity fund, which invests in designated low-income areas called opportunity zones. The tax on the gain is deferred for five years. Then 10% of the gain goes untaxed, or 30% if the fund keeps at least 90% of its assets in rural zones. Hold the fund at least 10 years, and its growth is tax-free when you sell, though growth after its 30th year is taxed.

Industry observers note that say a fund at least holds its value, and you put a $200,000 gain from a 2027 stock sale into it. Your 2032 return reports $180,000 of that gain, and that tax comes due while the fund still holds your money. Sell after 10 years, in 2037 at the earliest, and the fund’s growth is tax-free.

Sources indicate that the switch to the fresh rules makes timing matter. Gains already deferred under the old rules become taxable on Dec. 31, 2026, and IRS guidance bars rolling them into a new fund. A 2026 gain whose 180 days run into January 2027 can wait and go in under the new rules.

Only the gain qualifies, so any extra money you add counts as a separate investment with no tax break. Getting the full break also means leaving your money in projects in low-income areas for a decade, and the manager’s fees cut your return. The state securities regulators’ association warns that you could escape the tax and still lose your whole investment.

Recent findings suggest that so judge the fund as an investment first. Read what it will build and where, look up its manager and anyone selling it to you on FINRA’s BrokerCheck, and get every fee in writing.

Before you sign, ask whether you’d buy the fund with no tax break, and walk away if the answer is no.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, before you invest in a real estate syndication, vet the sponsor, not just its projected returns. Ask how its past deals did when rates jumped, how much of its own money is in this one, and whether the loan’s rate can rise with the market. Commit only money you can leave in for five to seven years.

A syndication’s projected returns are the sponsor’s own forecast, and the sponsor collects fees whether or not they come true.

It has been revealed that A syndication pools money from passive investors, the limited partners, to buy one large property, such as an apartment complex, and borrows the rest of the price. The sponsor runs it and typically sells after five to seven years. It earns an acquisition fee when it buys, an asset management fee each year, and a promote, often 20% to 30% of the profit above a set yearly return investors get first, called the preferred return. Only the promote depends on how investors do, so the sponsor’s skill and honesty matter more than the projections.

It has been revealed that while rates were low, the syndicator Tides Equities bought apartments with floating-rate loans, whose interest rises with market rates. Its rate caps, which limit how high the rate can go, lasted only two or three years. When its first loans came due, rates had jumped, and Tides couldn’t afford newly introduced caps or a refinance, The Real Deal reported. Lenders foreclosed on some of its complexes, and anyone with $50,000 in one of those deals lost all of it.

It has been revealed that vet the sponsor yourself, even when a real estate investing platform lists the deal. Ask it to show you:.

Industry observers note that then check the deal. For a floating-rate loan, ask when the rate cap runs out and when the loan comes due. Compare the rents and sale price the sponsor assumes with what similar buildings rent and sell for now. Also find out whether the sponsor can make a capital call, a demand for more money, and what happens to investors who can’t pay.

Size your stake so you could leave it alone for seven years and still afford a capital call.

Your car’s model and age set its starting resale price, but buyers then grade its condition and check its records, and you control much of both. Keep every service receipt, fix a flaw only when the repair costs less than the next condition grade adds to the price, and sell before a redesign or a massive scheduled service.

Industry observers note that kelley Blue Book values a used car at one of four condition grades, Excellent, Very Good, Good, or Fair, and each step down lowers the price. Half the cars it values land at Good.

According to recent reports, tires and paperwork help set the grade. Kelley Blue Book’s Very Good grade calls for matching tires with at least 75% of their tread and most service records, while Good asks for at least half the tread and some records.

So the grades tell you which repairs pay. Price the car in Kelley Blue Book’s value tool at its honest grade and one grade up, as a trade-in or a private sale, whichever you initiative. Spend on dent repair, professional detailing, or new tires only when the work costs less than the difference.

Until you sell, three habits protect the price:.

Brand and color are set for good, but fuel prices move. With fuel costs high in the third quarter of 2026, Cox Automotive found the wholesale prices dealers paid for large pickups and SUVs falling and those for EVs and smaller, fuel-efficient cars rising. So list a large pickup or SUV while gas is cheap.

Sell before a massive scheduled service, such as replacing the timing belt, comes due, since a buyer will subtract its cost from the offer.

Automakers reveal a redesign months before it goes on sale, and the new version draws buyers from yours, so list your car before it arrives.

  • According to recent reports, most first-time buyers put down less than 20%.
  • According to recent reports, twenty percent is only the point where a conventional loan, one without government backing, stops requiring private mortgage insurance (PMI), which protects the lender if you stop paying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that buying a home doesn’t take 20% down. Many loans take as little as 3% or 3.5%, and VA loans for veterans and USDA loans for some rural buyers need no down payment. Set aside your cash for closing costs, moving, and emergencies first, then put down what’s left and weigh the mortgage insurance a smaller down payment adds.

According to recent reports, most first-time buyers put down less than 20%. Their median down payment was 9% in the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 buyer survey.

According to recent reports, twenty percent is only the point where a conventional loan, one without government backing, stops requiring private mortgage insurance (PMI), which protects the lender if you stop paying. A smaller down payment can also mean a higher interest rate. You can ask to drop PMI once you owe 80% of the home’s original value. Government-insured FHA loans keep their mortgage insurance for the life of the loan when you put down less than 10%.

Recent findings suggest that on a $350,000 home, 5% down is $17,500, against $70,000 for 20%. Freddie Mac estimates PMI at $30 to $70 a month per $100,000 borrowed, or roughly $100 to $230 a month on the $332,500 loan, a cost to weigh against the $52,500 you’d keep. Waiting costs something too. Home prices rose 2.4% in the year through August 2026, the Federal Housing Finance Agency reports. At that pace, if saving the other $52,500 takes three years, the same house will cost about $376,000, and 20% of it about $75,000. Buying sooner with less down avoids that rise, as long as your savings stay intact.

Start from the lowest down payment your loan allows, on a home that appraises for at least its price.

Then set aside closing costs, typically 2% to 5% of the price, money for moving and repairs, and an emergency fund covering three to six months of essential bills. Whatever is left goes toward the down payment, and down payment assistance programs can help you reach your loan’s minimum. Ask lenders to quote your monthly payment at 5% and 10% down.

PMI can come off later, but cash you put into the house comes back out only if you borrow against it or sell.

Compare the best mortgage lenders for a loan that fits the down payment you choose.

#56706. Loud Wealth vs. Stealth Wealth: Why Materialism Fades Over Time

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1459 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

Loud Wealth vs. Stealth Wealth: Why Materialism Fades Over Time

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1459 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I’m a proponent of stealth wealth.
  • Stealth wealth is also the natural endgame of following FIRE principles for decades.
  • So by default, every long-term FIRE practitioner eventually becomes a stealth wealth practitioner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I’m a proponent of stealth wealth. It makes for a more peaceful life with lower expectations and less scrutiny. The last thing you want to do is show off and put you and your family in danger.

Stealth wealth is also the natural endgame of following FIRE principles for decades. If you keep living well below your means, which is required to retire early, your investments will eventually compound faster than you can spend.

So by default, every long-term FIRE practitioner eventually becomes a stealth wealth practitioner. Whether they mean to or not.

In private, you can do whatever you want. But in public, staying low-key is better. Here are three simple steps to follow:.

Recent findings suggest that 1) Dress simply. No designer brands or fancy outfits. Clean, comfortable clothes are all you need. Think jeans, t-shirt, warm jacket, sweater, sneakers, baseball hat.

Industry observers note that 2) Drive an old car. Driving a new car is stressful and can attract unwanted attention. If you insist on a luxury brand, try to keep it for at least 10 years.

Recent findings suggest that 3) Stay quiet about your spending on social media. Don't post vacation photos or the nice things you buy. If a tree falls in Hawaii and nobody sees it on Instagram, did the vacation still happen? Yes, and it was more relaxing.

Do these three things and you’ll join the Stealth Wealth club, a group of operators who move in and out of the shadows unnoticed.

Once you’re in, you’ll realize there are far more members than you think. That realization is oddly bullish. A lot more people are doing better than the media or politicians would have you believe. They’re just not wearing it.

In 8th grade in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, I wanted two things: to be cool and to have girlfriends.

My parents drove a 1976 Datsun with missing hubcaps. Getting dropped off in that car was social agony. So I had to find status elsewhere.

Sources indicate that at the time, there were two ways to increase your coolness as a teenager: be a good skateboarder or dress in designer clothes. I chose both.

Recent findings suggest that I still remember forking over 160 ringgit, about $64 back then (roughly $150 today), for a used pair of Armani Exchange jeans. 30-inch waist, 31-inch cut length, bronze eagle triangle on the back pocket. That was an absurd amount of money for a 13-year-old to spend on pants. But all the cool rich kids had them, so I had to have them too.

Then came the equally expensive Doc Martens. Then a Guess shirt. Looking back, nearly all my work and allowance money went to clothes and shoes.

Sources indicate that and you know what? I enjoyed it. It made me feel good, and I was part of the cool crowd with plenty of friends.

Industry observers note that today, I couldn’t give two shitake mushrooms about designer labels. I want comfortable, practical clothes with zipper pockets so I don’t lose my wallet, phone, and keys. I cut my own hair to save time and money, and I usually cover it with a frayed baseball cap anyway.

So what happened between Armani jeans and black running pants?

I stopped needing respect from everyone.

I’m writing this post because of a clip from author Min Jin Lee explaining why some people with little money spend lavishly on material things. As personal finance enthusiasts, we shake our heads at such conspicuous spending. Don’t they want to eventually be financially free? We think to ourselves. But we’re missing something important.

Her point: when you grow up in a poor community, respect matters enormously. It becomes a kind of currency. And when you don’t have much else, you tend to overvalue it. So you buy the nicer clothes, shoes, watches, and cars, hoping they command respect, even if it means carrying credit card debt.

Sources indicate that this resonated with me as a minority who came to America for high school and faced various racist incidents. Racism is one of the deepest forms of disrespect because you're insulted just for being who you are. Respect, especially for elders, is a major part of Asian culture. When people disrespect me online or in real life, it can be infuriating. In my younger years, I’d go after them to defend my honor.

According to recent reports, when you think about it this way, materialism isn’t irrational. It’s a logical strategy for buying respect when you don’t have other ways to earn it. With this understanding, I'm going to try and be extra respectful to everybody I interact with from now on.

Industry observers note that at 13, I spent a fortune on Armani jeans to earn respect from my skater friends and the girls I liked. When I started working in finance, I dressed to earn respect from my peers and bosses.

It has been revealed that then I left finance in 2012. Overnight, the nice clothes went untouched. I no longer needed respect from anyone outside my home.

Funny enough, they're all still hanging in my closet 14 years later in pristine condition.

Today, insults from random folks feel more like pinches instead of body blows. The passive income is doing its job as a shield.

In a recent development, as a dad now, the only people I want respect from are my wife and children. Having respect from my parents and sister would be nice too, but we don’t see each other day-to-day so it’s no major deal if not. As any parent and provider knows, taking care of a family is hard work.

As a result, on our family trip to Las Vegas, I confess that a part of me felt disrespected when my wife gave me a bothersome look when I asked her to take a few more profile photos of me at Redrocks.

Sources indicate that in that moment, my brain immediately pulled up the receipts. I agreed to this $7,000 trip despite being in a liquidity crunch. I went to bed at 2 am and still woke up by 6 am to get everyone breakfast. What’s the major deal?

Yes, I realize feeling disrespected in that moment might sound ridiculous. But that’s the point. A man wants to feel respected by his wife and children he provides for.

Industry observers note that reaching FIRE doesn’t eliminate the desire for respect. It just shrinks the circle of people whose respect you care about. The flip side is that when you don’t get respect from the few people who matter most, it stings far more than any stranger’s opinion ever could.

It’s worth doing an honest self-assessment of your spending on material things.

Maybe you genuinely love watches, cars, clothes, shoes, jewelry, or handbags. That’s fine, as long as you can comfortably pay cash and never carry a revolving credit card balance.

But if you’re buying expensive things you don’t even use or love, you may still be chasing status to earn respect.

Sources indicate that maybe the midlife sports car is compensating for something. Maybe the designer wardrobe is a response to someone who once made an unkind comment about your body. Or maybe the nonstop social media highlight reel is an attempt to prove the middle school bullies wrong.

Whatever the reason, it’s worth exploring. Because the people you’re trying to impress are probably too busy trying to impress someone else. Know that there is an incredible joy of being a nobody so long as you have your finances in order.

For many of us in the FIRE community, the desire for stuff fades over time because the need for outside respect fades too. Once you’re living the life you want and own the things you need, strangers have nothing left to grant you. Nobody can hand you a better life than the one you’ve already built.

That’s the real luxury of stealth wealth. Not hiding your money, but no longer needing an audience for it.

It has been revealed that readers, did you go through a loud wealth phase when you were younger? What was your version of the Armani jeans? Do you think materialism is really about respect, or is something else going on? And now that you’re older, whose respect do you still care about, and how do you feel when you don’t get it?

Sources indicate that stealth wealth means nobody else needs to know your net worth. But you should.

It has been revealed that people spend thousands on designer clothes to impress strangers. A free expert review of your finances is a far better flex, even if nobody sees it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As executor, settle the estate in order: get the court’s authority, inventory everything, and pay valid debts, taxes, and costs from an estate account before you distribute anything.
  • Family members may press for their shares within weeks, long before it’s safe to pay them.
  • In a recent development, federal taxes come first when an estate can’t pay all its debts, according to IRS Publication 559.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As executor, settle the estate in order: get the court’s authority, inventory everything, and pay valid debts, taxes, and costs from an estate account before you distribute anything. If you hand out inheritances first and the estate runs short, the IRS can hold you personally responsible for the tax it still owes.

Family members may press for their shares within weeks, long before it’s safe to pay them.

In a recent development, federal taxes come first when an estate can’t pay all its debts, according to IRS Publication 559. An executor who pays heirs ahead of a tax debt they knew of, or should have known of, owes it personally, up to the amount paid out ahead of it.

Hire a probate lawyer if the estate can’t cover its debts or an heir contests the will. Skip the executor’s fee if you’re the only heir, since the fee is taxable income and an inheritance isn’t.

In a recent development, say a daughter and her brother inherit their father’s estate in equal shares, and she’s the executor. Over nine months she pays $20,000 of his final bills and taxes from the estate’s $250,000, and only then splits the remaining $230,000, $115,000 each.

Industry observers note that send IRS Form 5495 right after you file the final returns. The IRS then has nine months to name any tax due, and paying it ends your personal liability for those taxes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that make your savings goal hard to quit with a commitment device, a choice you lock in now so that backing out later takes effort or costs money. Use the least restrictive one that keeps you saving, and give the goal a dollar amount and a deadline so the device has something to hold you to.

Sources indicate that you set a savings goal on a day when saving feels easy. You keep it, or don’t, on harder days, when a sale or a short paycheck makes skipping one deposit look harmless.

A commitment device makes the decision for those days in advance. Ulysses had his crew tie him to the mast so he could hear the Sirens’ song without steering toward them. With money, the device removes the tempting option, or puts a price on it, before temptation arrives.

According to recent reports, economists Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi built one into a retirement initiative. In their Save More Tomorrow program, workers agreed in advance to save part of each future raise. At the first company to offer it, participants’ average saving rate rose from 3.5% of pay to 13.6% in 40 months.

Pick a device that fits the goal:.

Industry observers note that start with the least restrictive device that keeps you saving. A penalty so steep that you hesitate to put money in leaves you saving nothing.

Give the goal an amount and a date, such as $2,400 by Oct. 1, so you and any referee know what counts as keeping it.

Set up one device this week, and keep the stricter ones for goals you’ve already broken once.

Compare the best high-yield savings accounts to choose where the goal’s money will sit.
