The Shockingly Simple Math Behind Social Security

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the world of very early retirement, we tend to ignore one of the most vital things for normal retirees: the Social Security program.
  • Don’t get me wrong, it’s a great thing for the 73 million people who presently draw benefits, and it provides an essential safety net for many who don’t have much income from anywhere else.
  • But for those of us leaving the workplace in our 30 and 40s, Social Security is just a fuzzy concept in the very distant future.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the world of very early retirement, we tend to ignore one of the most vital things for normal retirees: the Social Security program.

Don’t get me wrong, it’s a great thing for the 73 million people who presently draw benefits, and it provides an essential safety net for many who don’t have much income from anywhere else.

But for those of us leaving the workplace in our 30 and 40s, Social Security is just a fuzzy concept in the very distant future. We aren’t thinking about money that eases us into our Golden Years, we need something that starts working now. Plus we’d rather not rely on our government keeping its promises that far into the future.

Recent findings suggest that those were my thoughts in 2005, when I was just a young retiree myself. But a funny thing happens when time passes: you get older. And you realize that there are plenty of other older people around too. And suddenly, Social Security is an notable subject after all, that many people would like to know more about. But there is an endless pile of conflicting opinions:.

But when I did the math on all of this, I realized that it’s more confusing than it needs to be. Because when it comes to deciding on how Social Security fits into your retirement strategy, it really boils down to only one number:.

The Net Present Value of your future lifetime stream of Social Security payments.

Industry observers note that that little piece of math jargon might not mean much if you don’t have fond memories of  Economics 101 class. But don’t worry, it’s easy to understand if you think of these two extremes:.

If you want to retire in your 30s like I did, the value of your future Social Security is pretty close to zero. Even if the government keeps all of its promises, those payments are so far in the future that you need to save a full retirement ‘stash to get through the three decades until it kicks in.

On the other hand, if you’re already over 60 years old, contributed to Social Security throughout your long career and have a low cost of living, you may be eligible for payments that already meet all your needs.

In this situation, you are set for life. Social Security will in theory cover all your needs and rise automatically with inflation, so you don’t have to save any additional money.

In between these two extremes, the math gets interesting. Because while most people assume Social Security is useless until you reach full eligibility, the real story is that you can think of it as a chunk of money that you already have right now, which reduces the amount of saving you have to do on your own.

And there’s an easy way to calculate it, with an extremely useful thing called the Net Present Value calculation.

There’s an actual formula for this, but don’t worry you don’t have to memorize it because you can just have any Internet calculator, AI tool or spreadsheet do the math for you.

In a recent development, first let’s calculate the value a young couple might get if they do this calculation at 30 years old. We just have to make a few assumptions to have numbers plug into the formula:.

Sources indicate that when you plug in all the numbers and calculate this (the Net Present Value of a 30 year stream of income), the first number you’ll get is $667,166. But that’s not the final answer – that is how much you’d need if you wanted the payments to start right now.

The final step is applying a simpler version of the formula a second time, to account for the fact that you don’t need the money until 32 years from now:.

Sources indicate that at that point, you end up with a number around $98,280. But what does this mean?

It means that if you stuck $98k into an investment account today and let it compound for 32 years, at that point it would be big enough to provide a stream of $4000 payments for the following 30 years. And this even takes future inflation into account!It also means that the 30 year old retirees can mark an imaginary $98k onto their “net worth” spreadsheet and save that much less. Or at least think of it as a nice safety margin.

If you’re latest to money and math, that may sound like sorcery, but if you’ve been investing for long enough you will understand that it really does work that way. So let’s re-run the example for a couple who is already 62 years old, and needs a $5000 income starting right now, that still needs to last 30 years.

That NPV calculation looks like this:.

And the answer is right around $834,000.

Recent findings suggest that what this means, is that if they invested $834,000 into a fund that paid out 6% per year for 30 years before running dry, they’d get that exact same $5000 monthly income. And it would keep up with inflation.

Now that we’ve seen these examples from the extreme ends of the spectrum, we can see how this applies in a more typical situation. Here’s one that is loosely based on one from a real person I worked with last year:.

Shane Survivor is 55 and he has been through some hard times. He lost most of his savings in a business blowup a few years back, but really wishes he could still retire soon. His financial picture:.

Most financial advisors would tell him to tough it out and  just keep working until he hits Social Security eligibility. At least 62 to get the minimum benefits, but maybe even longer to get to Full Retirement Age (67) or even until 70 to get the maximum benefit.

But wait! Let’s do the math because who wants to work another fifteen years when you’re already tired of working at 55!

Shane logs into the Social Security website SSA.gov and uses the online tool to calculate what his payout will be. I just did this myself so we can use my numbers:.

Let’s start by calculating the Net Present Value of each of these three options for our 55-year old friend:.

Industry observers note that whoa wait a minute, that’s a counterintuitive result! Am I really telling you that it’s actually less valuable to work longer so you can get the higher benefits? The answer is yes, for people who understand the concepts of “investing” and “the time value of money”.

To really understand this, just imagine what would happen if you started taking those payments as early as possible (age 62) and tossed them into an index fund, earning 6% after inflation on average. After the first year, you’d already have about $24,300 and you’d still be piling in that extra two grand per month and the whole snowball would be starting to compound.

By the time your more patient friends started drawing $2796 payments five years later, you’d already have over $137,000. It’s such a massive lead that the 67-year-old will never catch up.

But let’s go back to Shane’s real situation and see if he can retire:.

Sources indicate that so the answer is no, not quite yet. But he’s closer than it looks: every year of additional work will have a triple effect because it will:.

As soon as his combined ‘stash investment income plus the Social Security payment reach $3000 per month, he’s done.

In a recent development, and of course, any additional tricks he can apply like streamlining his spending and boosting his income, will make this even faster. I’d give him about three years before reaching liftoff.

So how can YOU use this information to speed up your own retirement?

In a recent development, the net effect of Social Security is that it should help you worry a little less and work a little less. The worrying part should benefit everyone, and the working part is kind of a sliding scale:.

Can we just put this in ONE SIMPLE TABLE based on some reasonable assumptions?

Sources indicate that yes, absolutely! Just to hit the most common situation, let’s assume a household that has.

How much is this future benefit worth you you, based on your current age?

These aren’t enormous FAT Fire numbers, but every one of them is enough to feel like a meaningful contribution to your eventual early jump into freedom. For example as a 51-year-old, I can look at my number of roughly $350,000 and say yeah, that’s quite a significant boost – enough to buy an entire house in many areas of the country or enough to fund multiple lifetimes of high-end groceries. And until now I had never even considered it as part of my retirement savings!

Frequently Asked (or Complained) Questions.

Now that we’ve covered the facts, I can already hear the complaints coming.

What if Social Security is canceled or greatly reduced by the time I reach that age?

Sources indicate that yeah, it might happen, but it’s also a top priority for most voters in our aging population. So it’s hard for politicians to make cuts. What is more likely is that the benefits will be cut for wealthier people. And if you find yourself in that camp (as I do), you won’t actually need the payments.

According to recent reports, sure, it’s not “fair”, but you know what? I can think of more fun ways to enjoy the fact that I’m a rich person rather than complaining about how some government program is “unfair”, and so can you.

Nobody can live on just a Social Security check!

First of all, millions of people do. In fact, last time I checked my own annual spending it was under $30k, most of it on optional luxuries, which is less than my expected payout!

But more importantly, most of us won’t have to, because we are also investing healthy sums on our own.

I’m still scared and worried about something else!

Recent findings suggest that now this is the root of the issue. In fact, worry is the root of almost all challenges. And so that’s what we need to focus on in our future work. For some reason, I have managed to live the last twenty years pretty much completely free from financial worries, and I had assumed everyone else was the same way. But it turns out this is not the case, even among people much wealthier and more advantaged than I am.

So in the next article, we need to get into that.

Sources indicate that log yourself into ssa.gov, and if it’s your first time doing that – congratulations! Note that newly introduced users will need to create an account, and they’ll guide you to login.gov for that purpose. Don’t fret, it’s very useful to have this account for multiple reasons.

Bonus Materials: the Quirk of Social Security Contributions.

To illustrate this point, I ran a simulation of two people who each make a $100k salary and contribute accordingly, but one retires after 10 years and that poor second guy works the full 35. Look at the difference in their benefits:.

So the early retiree only worked and contributed about 28% as much as the late retiree. But his benefits are still a much higher 45% of the big earner’s payouts. In summary? Social Security provides a mild incentive for slacking.

Sources indicate that one other factor: after retiring earlier, you might still end up contributing more than you think. This is because any income you earn later in life through optional employment (or self employment) will trigger more contributions. In my 21 years of retirement, I have ended up earning and contributing more during about 15 of those years, bringing my average level up much higher than I originally expected.

Final Tip: If in doubt, ask your Favorite AI.

Industry observers note that even though this has become a long article, it is still far from a complete analysis of the Social Security program. How Much Allowance to Give – Start With Age, Then Add Up What It Covers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (438 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Start your child’s allowance near $1 a week per year of age, then adjust it for what it has to cover.
  • Next to what other parents report paying, that age rule can look stingy.
  • In a 2025 Wells Fargo survey, the median weekly allowance, the middle of what parents reported, came in above the age rule for every age group:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Start your child’s allowance near $1 a week per year of age, then adjust it for what it has to cover. Add up what you now spend each week on the things it will pay for, so the allowance replaces that money. Pay it on a fixed day, and raise it as they take on new costs.

Next to what other parents report paying, that age rule can look stingy.

In a 2025 Wells Fargo survey, the median weekly allowance, the middle of what parents reported, came in above the age rule for every age group:.

Paying less than those medians doesn’t make you stingy, because what the allowance pays for sets the right amount. One that buys only treats can stay near the age rule, while one that also covers school lunches or clothes has to be bigger.

Industry observers note that list what your child will now buy with it, and add up what you spend on those things in a typical week. Make that total the allowance and stop buying those things yourself, so it replaces money you already spend instead of adding a newly introduced cost. When the money runs out early, let them run short until payday instead of topping it up. Whether to tie it to chores is a separate decision.

Say your 10-year-old takes over paying for their snacks, small toys, and outings with friends, which cost you about $10 a week. Their allowance is $10. By 13, a $1 raise on each birthday brings it to $13, and handing over their clothes budget, about $50 a month, adds about $12 a week, for $25 in all.

Pay it on the same day every week, and raise it on each birthday and the week it takes on a new cost. Cash, which most parents in the survey use, lets a young child see and count what’s left. A kids’ debit card can pay it on a schedule and alert you to their purchases through its app.

Write the list down before the first payday, so you and your child both know which purchases are now theirs.

  • In most states, managing rentals for other owners takes a real estate broker’s license or a property management license, the Bureau of Labor Statistics says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you take on a single client, get the real estate broker’s or property management license your state requires for managing other owners’ rentals. Then form a limited liability company, insure the business, open a trust account for owners’ rents and tenants’ deposits, and keep adding homes to manage until the fees pay you a salary.

Rental owners pay a manager to fill vacancies, collect rent, and handle repairs, and a management manufacturer can start with a single owner’s house.

In most states, managing rentals for other owners takes a real estate broker’s license or a property management license, the Bureau of Labor Statistics says. Maine’s real estate commission, for one, says rental management needs no real estate license there, so check with your own state’s real estate commission before you advertise.

Managers typically charge 8% to 12% of the rent they collect, the National Association of Residential Property Managers says. Most also charge a leasing fee each time they place a fresh tenant, and many charge another when a lease renews. Say you manage 40 single-family homes that stay rented all year at an average rent of $1,800, and you charge 9%. Each home pays you $162 a month, or about $77,800 a year for all 40, before leasing fees and the costs of running the business.

Sources indicate that ask real estate agents who don’t manage rentals, and rental investors you know, to refer owners to you. Each owner hires you to screen tenants, collect rent, hire repair crews, inspect the home, and file evictions, all under fair housing law and your state’s security deposit rules.

Industry observers note that put your monthly fee, your leasing fee, and the most you’ll spend on a repair without the owner’s approval in a written management agreement. Then have a real estate attorney in your state review it before your first owner signs.

#56698. Getting Rich Is Easy Compared To Finding And Keeping Love

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

Getting Rich Is Easy Compared To Finding And Keeping Love

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a parent, I have two main concerns for my children.
  • Will they be able to earn a livable wage in a world where AI keeps eating entry-level jobs?
  • In a recent development, A net worth target gets more achievable the more you save and the more time goes by.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a parent, I have two main concerns for my children.

The first is economic stability. Will they be able to earn a livable wage in a world where AI keeps eating entry-level jobs? I question the time and money we spend educating our kids all the time. So I've been aggressively saving and investing for their future, just in case.

The second concern is bigger. Will my children find love?

In a recent development, A net worth target gets more achievable the more you save and the more time goes by. Compounding is boring, but it's reliable. If the direction is correct, sooner or later you will get there.

Industry observers note that finding a partner is far more amorphous. Our kids can work on their communication skills, fitness, charm, education, hygiene, empathy, and finances. But all of that merely improves their odds. There are no guarantees.

Which brings me to the strangest business story of 2026.

Sources indicate that in late October, The Newly introduced York Times reported that U.S. officials concluded a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a Chinese intelligence asset. She is a senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center manufacturer and Nvidia cloud partner that rents computing power to Chinese firms.

Recent findings suggest that surveillance of her reportedly revealed a close relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. And no, they are not related. Huang is a common surname like Smith.

According to recent reports, the Financial Times then reported that a U.S. government memo described the relationship as romantic. Her alleged goal was to gather information on Jensen and advanced AI chips, and to nudge him to lobby for looser chip exports to China.

It has been revealed that the allegations come from anonymous officials and haven't been tested publicly. Officials reportedly don't believe Jensen knew about any intelligence activity. Nvidia claims his interactions with her were routine customer meetings. China denies the whole thing. House Republican committee chairs want a closed-door briefing on November 18.

Recent findings suggest that so nobody outside the room knows the full story, except that Jensen admitted to the affair and is no longer CEO as of November 23, 2026. The lessons about love and money are worth discussing regardless of how the facts shake out.

Jensen Huang is worth over $120 billion (once $170 billion). He runs a company worth about $4 trillion after the sell-off. He is the closest thing we have to a modern-day emperor, the face of the AI revolution, mobbed like a rock star everywhere he goes in Taiwan.

And yet, if the reporting is accurate, it still wasn't enough.

It has been revealed that there's a line from Gemma Teller Morrow in the TV show, Sons of Anarchy: “Only men need to be loved, sweetheart. Women need to be wanted.”.

In a recent development, it's not entirely true. Everybody wants to be loved and desired to some degree. But the line points to something uncomfortable. No amount of money, applause, or leather jackets fills the need to feel admired by one specific person who seems to see you.

We all just want to be loved and accepted for who we are.

Here's the twist that makes this story sadder.

According to recent reports, if U.S. officials are right, what may have felt like admiration was tradecraft. Attentiveness, respect, and flattery are exactly what an intelligence service would deploy against the most vital man in AI. Intelligence services have used romance as an opening for as long as there have been secrets worth stealing.

Which exposes the hidden problem of extreme wealth and power. The richer you get, the harder it becomes to know whether anyone loves you for you. Every new person in your life has a reason to be nice to you. Normal people get to skip that existential headache.

Sources indicate that money doesn't make finding love easier. Past a certain point, it makes find true love harder.

The people worth keeping are the ones who liked you before you were worth liking.

Jensen is far from the first emperor to create a commotion over love for a woman.

Paris and Helen of Troy. The Greeks' foundational story is about a prince who ran off with another man's wife and got his entire city burned to the ground. Myth, sure. But the Greeks clearly understood the risk.

Mark Antony and Cleopatra. Antony controlled half the Roman world. He chose Cleopatra over Rome, lost at Actium in 31 BC, and both were dead within a year. Octavian got the empire.

Industry observers note that king Edward VIII. In 1936, he abdicated the British throne after less than a year to marry Wallis Simpson, a twice-divorced American. He traded a kingdom for love, and spent the rest of his life in comfortable, irrelevant exile.

John Profumo. The closest parallel to the Jensen story. In 1963, Britain's Secretary of State for War was revealed to have had an affair with Christine Keeler, who was also involved with a Soviet naval attaché. Profumo lied to Parliament, resigned in disgrace, and the scandal helped bring down the government.

Brian Krzanich. Intel's CEO resigned in 2018 after a past consensual relationship with an employee came to light. Running a chip giant doesn't come with an exemption.

Industry observers note that jeff Bezos. His 2019 divorce after 25 years of marriage sent roughly 4% of Amazon, worth about $38 billion at the time, to MacKenzie Scott. Bezos kept his job, married Lauren Sánchez, and is still one of the richest men alive. But it was the most expensive breakup in history.

Industry observers note that the pattern is clear. Kingdoms, careers, and fortunes are rebuildable. However, once you find the one, you will do anything to get them.

In a recent development, remember Indecent Proposal from 1993? Robert Redford’s billionaire character offers a struggling couple, played by Demi Moore and Woody Harrelson, $1 million for one night with the wife. They take the deal. Their marriage nearly implodes.

The couple discovered they had a price, and it wasn’t that high. But they badly underestimated what they were selling.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, the billionaire could buy the night. He couldn’t buy her heart. He had everything except the one thing he actually wanted.

Recent findings suggest that swap Redford for any modern tech billionaire and the lesson holds. Money can buy almost anything. Except the feeling of being genuinely loved.

The lack of money is a solvable problem.

Plenty of regular people have become millionaires this way. The formula is public.

Sources indicate that there is no formula for love. You can do everything right and still never meet the one. And even if you do, roughly 40% of first marriages in America end in divorce. Finding love involves tremendous luck. Keeping it is work.

According to recent reports, you can always make another dollar. You can't always make another soulmate.

According to recent reports, in 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General declared loneliness an epidemic. About half of American adults report feeling lonely, and the health impact of social disconnection was compared to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day.

The FIRE crowd isn't immune. Early retirement can be isolating. Your friends are at work. Your identity is gone. And if you're married, there's a specific trap worth sharing.

FIRE is better when both partners retire and experience freedom together. Not when one spouse is slaving away while the other is kicking back. Resentment will surely kick in.

Recent findings suggest that yes, I get it. Some men’s egos still need protecting when their wives are bringing home the sashimi. But men need to get over themselves. Women now make up the majority of college students, and plenty of them will out-earn their husbands.

Industry observers note that I left banking in 2012. My wife kept working until 2015 when she negotiated her own severance. For almost three years, I was the guy at home while she commuted.

Industry observers note that if you're planning FIRE, plan a joint exit. Life is better this way.

1) A high-value spouse may need more respect just to break even. If your partner is successful, attractive, or powerful, the world is constantly praising them. Next to all that adoration, treating them normally at home can inadvertently feel like a lack of respect, or even disrespect. So you may have to deliberately show more appreciation than feels natural just to run in place.

2) Everything gets taken for granted. Eat Kobe beef every day and you’ll get sick of it. In FIRE land, wake up without an alarm clock every day and you’ll take that for granted too. The antidote is voluntary discomfort. Scrub your own toilets after a major investment win. Take a part-time consulting gig a 40-minute bus ride away that makes you take orders from a micromanager. Practice fasting for at least 18 hours once a month if you have access to unlimited food. Doing uncomfortable things on purpose helps you appreciate the people you already have.

Recent findings suggest that 3) Privacy is priceless. When you’re private, you can fix your mistakes without the whole world watching. Being known in your small circle for something good is great. Being famous means millions of strangers have opinions about who you are. Respond to all of them and you’ll never have peace of mind. Embrace being a rich nobody.

Sources indicate that whatever the full truth turns out to be, this whole situation is sad. Sad for Lori and their adult children. Sad for Jensen and his legacy. Disappointing for Nvidia’s tens of thousands of employees and shareholders like me. And a blow for America, given we’re in a global AI race.

Sources indicate that relationships are hard. They require constant work and attentiveness. Forty years of marriage doesn’t buy you immunity. If anything, it makes it easier to stop paying attention.

It has been revealed that if there’s one silver lining, it’s that this story may help bring the left and the right together on maintaining our lead in AI. AI spending has been one of the biggest drivers of U.S. economic growth. If post-midterm infighting causes us to lose the race, we could sink the economy along with it.

If someone with that much money and goodwill was allegedly willing to risk throwing it away, you can’t really blame people for their emotions and their desire to be loved. We’re all human.

Besides a basic amount of financial security, I hope my kids will find someone who will support, love, and cherish them. I would rather my kids find that person than be rich.

Money can help protect them after I’m gone. But money can’t hug them after a bad day, sit with them in a hospital waiting room, or celebrate their wins with them. Knowing they each have someone like that is what will let me rest easy. That’s when I’ll know my kids will be OK.

Then I hope they never take that person for granted. Because the odds say they will, just like most of us take for granted the water we drink and the air we breathe.

Readers, do you agree that making money is easier than finding love? Would you take the $1 million in Indecent Proposal, or $2.2 million in today's dollars? If you've achieved FIRE, did you and your spouse exit together, or did one of you keep working, and how did that affect your relationship? And if you had $140+ billion, how would you ever know if someone loved you for you?

If you're a worried parent, I'm diligently working on my latest book out in Fall 2027, Your Kids Will Be OK: Smart Money Decisions For Parents In An Uncertain World, published by Portfolio Penguin. It's about raising capable, resilient kids and making solid money decisions so they have a real shot at independence, and at a good life.

You can’t buy love, but you can protect it. If your family depends on your income, term life insurance is one of the most loving financial moves you can make.

My wife and I each got matching 20-year term policies through Policygenius after shopping around for months. It took far less time than I expected, and we sleep better knowing our kids would be OK if the unthinkable happened. Check out Policygenius to compare quotes from top insurers for free.

In a recent development, stocks can swing 20% on a single headline. Real estate tends to move more slowly, generate rental income, and give you something tangible to own. That’s why real estate has been a core part of my net worth for over 23 years, and it helps me sleep better when the stock market gets volatile.

According to recent reports, if you want real estate exposure without the hassle of being a landlord, check out Fundrise. It invests in a diversified portfolio of private real estate across the Sunbelt, including residential and industrial properties, and is expanding into data centers as demand for computing power grows. You can start with just $10.

It has been revealed that money is the easier problem to solve, and I’ve been helping readers solve it since 2009. Join 60,000+ others and get my free weekly newsletter here. I share what I’m seeing and doing with my own money, plus the lessons on family, freedom, and life that don’t fit neatly into a spreadsheet.

#56696. Checking Your Own Credit Never Lowers Your Score – Applying for Credit Can

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (462 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

Checking Your Own Credit Never Lowers Your Score – Applying for Credit Can

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (462 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that check your own credit report and score as often as you like, since your own checks are soft inquiries that never affect your score.
  • An inquiry is hard when a lender checks your credit because you applied to borrow from it.
  • According to FICO, a utility checking your credit to set a security deposit makes a soft inquiry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that check your own credit report and score as often as you like, since your own checks are soft inquiries that never affect your score. A hard inquiry, the check a lender makes when you apply for credit, can take a few points off your FICO scores for a year, so space your applications several months apart.

An inquiry is hard when a lender checks your credit because you applied to borrow from it. Nearly everything else is soft. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau lists your own requests for your reports, the checks behind pre-approved offers, your current lenders’ account reviews, and employment screening among soft inquiries. Those never affect your credit scores, and neither does checking whether a card issuer will pre-approve you before you apply.

According to FICO, a utility checking your credit to set a security deposit makes a soft inquiry. Most checks by phone carriers and landlords don’t affect your FICO scores either, though some can, depending on how the credit bureau has classified the carrier or landlord. And asking for a higher credit limit can mean a hard inquiry at some card issuers and a soft one at others.

In a recent development, even a hard inquiry costs little. FICO says one more takes less than five points off most people’s scores, and it counts for a year, though it stays on your report for up to two. Several at once weigh more than a single one, since a burst of applications makes it look as if you’re taking on more debt, and each hits harder when your credit history is short or holds few accounts. Rate shopping is the exception, because FICO treats several applications for one mortgage, car loan, or student loan as a single inquiry within a short window.

In a recent development, picture someone who checks her score every week in her card’s app and never loses a point. Then she applies for three store cards in one month, and her score dips, because each application added a hard inquiry.

So check your own credit as often as you like, starting with your reports from all three credit bureaus, free every week at AnnualCreditReport.com. Apply only for credit you need, and leave several months between applications.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The three-man Russian team returned to Everest’s West Ridge but found the route even more difficult than they expected. After two days of struggle, they’re heading back to Base Camp.

Recent findings suggest that on October 20, Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov went back up to the Lho La and pitched their tent on the wide plateau beyond. They still had time to fix more rope higher up.

“We moved…over terrain we’d already covered on the previous rotation,” the climbers texted to team member Natalya Belyankina, who had to abandon the expedition due to illness.

“The weather is good: sunny, with light winds, but cold,” they noted. “Progress was painfully slow today due to heavy packs and a persistent cough,” the climbers noted later.

It has been revealed that on Wednesday, they hoped to reach 7,500m, spend the night there, check the route ahead, and then retreat to the plateau. However, they didn’t get as far as they had planned.

Sources indicate that “We didn’t cover much ground today,” leader Andrei Vsiliev texted Anna Piunova of The Mountain Club. “The route is no walk in the park. We have to climb steep snowy slopes that conceal rock sections underneath.”.

According to recent reports, to make things worse, they found no suitable bivy spots at their highest point, so they had to retreat to a place where they could pitch their tent for the night. Today, they were just too exhausted to keep going.

Industry observers note that “We’re heading down; we’re sick and need to recover,” Vasiliev told Belyankina. “We can barely keep moving.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Find the conditions that waive your monthly checking fee and meet the easiest one, which may only mean sending part of your paycheck to the account.
  • A $15 monthly maintenance fee on checking costs $180 a year, for the kind of account many banks offer free.
  • Your account’s page on the bank’s website and its fee schedule list the ways to avoid the fee, and you may be close to meeting one already.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Find the conditions that waive your monthly checking fee and meet the easiest one, which may only mean sending part of your paycheck to the account. If none fits, ask the bank to move you to its basic account, or switch to a free checking account elsewhere.

A $15 monthly maintenance fee on checking costs $180 a year, for the kind of account many banks offer free.

Your account’s page on the bank’s website and its fee schedule list the ways to avoid the fee, and you may be close to meeting one already. Chase Total Checking, for example, charges $15 a month but nothing for a statement period with $500 in qualifying electronic deposits, such as a paycheck or government benefits.

A balance of at least $1,500 at the start of every day also waives the fee, and so does a $5,000 daily average, counting linked Chase savings and investments. The $1,500 balance is the easiest of the three to miss, since one day that starts below $1,500 rules that option out for the whole period.

In a recent development, say your paycheck goes to a credit union and your Chase account charges $15 a month. If your employer lets you split your direct deposit, send a fixed $500 of each paycheck to Chase and the rest to the credit union, and you save $180 a year. A Zelle transfer, cash, or a check won’t count toward the $500.

Sources indicate that if no condition fits, call the bank and ask to move to its basic account. Chase Secure Banking, for one, charges $4.95 a month but nothing for a statement period with $250 in qualifying electronic deposits, though it has no paper checks or outgoing wire transfers. On the same call, ask for the last few months’ fees back, along with any other fee you find by adding up a year of bank fees.

If you’d still pay a fee, open a free checking account at an online bank or credit union.

To pick one, compare the best free checking accounts.

#56693. Colorado Hiker Creates Ultimate Thru-Hike Across His Home State

📅 22 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1168 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Colorado Hiker Creates Ultimate Thru-Hike Across His Home State

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, donovan Rice got into thru-hiking almost by accident.
  • “I thought, there’s no way somebody can walk from Mexico to Canada.
  • Sources indicate that from there, it was a slippery slope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, donovan Rice got into thru-hiking almost by accident. Already outdoorsy, he graduated from long hikes to planning to climb all 53 of Colorado’s 14,000’ers (mountains above 14,000 feet, or 4,267m). While researching which peaks required overnight camping, he realized that some people’s hikes just keep going.

“I thought, there’s no way somebody can walk from Mexico to Canada. That’s just ridiculous,” Rice explained. “I fell in love with that idea.”.

Sources indicate that from there, it was a slippery slope. First came the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT), from the Mexican border in California to the Canadian border in British Columbia. Then he did the Continental Divide Trail (CDT), tracing the Rocky Mountains from Upcoming Mexico to the Montana-Canada border. Before he knew it, he had a trail name — Iceman —and was working the gig economy to free up time for wilderness adventures.

But that’s where most people’s slippery slope levels out. Hiking the 4,988km CDT is as meaty a project as most of us can imagine. But for Rice, it only opened the floodgates. He was fascinated by everything that didn’t make it into famous routes, especially the ridges and mountains he passed in his home state of Colorado that were just off trail.

“There’s all this stuff the CDT doesn’t hit because it is following the Continental Divide,” he told ExplorersWeb. “So when I got to the end of the Colorado section, about 700 miles, I was thinking, man, if there were a 2,000-mile version of that, it would be my dream thru-hike. Just that non-stop, relentless brutality that is Colorado.”.

Colorado has 14,000′ peaks but also deserts. Photo: Donovan Rice.

Rice started thinking about a massive thru-hike loop of the state. His idea was to stitch together existing trails and form upcoming ones where necessary.

Industry observers note that “I dropped a load of pins across the areas in Colorado I wanted to visit, then I pulled out a public lands layer of the map to see how I might connect the areas,” he explained. “The three core design philosophies were beauty, breadth, and epicness. I wanted to see beautiful views, I wanted to cover as much of Colorado’s diversity as possible, and I wanted to take the most iconic and epic route possible.”.

Recent findings suggest that unlike places like the UK, there is no “right to roam” in Colorado, so connecting the route to avoid private land was tricky. Occasionally, he had to link bits of public land and sections of trail in the “least worst way,” with short road walks when private property appeared to halt progress.

According to recent reports, as he tacked on mountain peaks and the national parks he wanted to explore, his route swelled to a monstrous 3,000km+. His itinerary now included all 11 of Colorado’s national forests, three of its national parks, 13 14,000’ers and 47 13,000’ers.

In a recent development, “This is not an efficient route,” Rice admits. “You could walk the full perimeter of Colorado and then hike the Colorado Trail [an existing 885km trail from Waterton Canyon near Denver to Durango], and then still have kilometers left over [to complete the loop].”.

The Great Colorado Route. Photo: Donovan Rice.

The route looked epic on paper, but Rice still needed to prove it could actually be thru-hiked. After months of planning, Rice set off on his Great Colorado Route from Gunnison National Park on May 14, 2026. He traveled ultra-light, carrying just six kilos of gear, with just a quilt instead of a sleeping bag and a tarp rather than a tent.

Sources indicate that “I wanted it to be lightweight enough that I could be nimble on the mountains while doing these technical traverses,” stated Rice. Traveling light was wise. Rice’s Great Colorado Route is challenging, with plenty of scrambling and sustained time at altitude.

Industry observers note that “The crux might be between Bailey and Rocky Mountain National Park. You go over the Mount Evans Wilderness, two 14,000’ers, hop on the Front Range across several 13,000’ers, and then across the Tenmile Range, and then the absolutely brutal Gore Range.”.

Rice spent 141 days tramping his trail, eventually finishing on October 1 after 3,252km. While he describes the route as “definitely not beginner-friendly” — due to plenty of cross-country terrain, off-trail navigation, and route-finding — it doesn’t require mountaineering skills.

“For me, the real sweet spot is Class three scrambling,” he says. “Once you get up to Class four, it starts getting really scary, and I had no tolerance at all for true Class five rock climbing.”.

Recent findings suggest that however, he did pack an ice ax, micro-spikes, snow gaiters, and a lightweight helmet to protect against rockfall. He also made an effort to structure the route to provide relief between the most challenging sections, giving the trail an ebb and flow, and potential hikers time to decompress.

In a recent development, the Ballard to La Junta traverse. Photo: Donovan Rice.

Sources indicate that overall, his focus on scenic beauty over contrived difficulty helped keep the route somewhat accessible. This is important because Rice hopes that other hikers will give it a go. He is building a website that maps the route, segment by segment, with GPS coordinates to help future hikers find the best places to camp or alternative paths depending on trail conditions. This is a May-through-October trail, but Rice stresses that it is unrealistic to expect perfect conditions for four and a half months.

It has been revealed that “This is one of those routes where bailouts will have to happen,” Rice explained. “You’ll have to take a low route or an alternate. I’m hoping to revisit some of the areas in the future and establish some of these alternative routes.”.

He aims to get all 29 segments of the initial route fully mapped on The Great Colorado website by the end of the year. It’s a big project, almost as big as the hike itself.

“I need to see how many people will actually give it a try. People can do segments. I’d love to see more thru-hikers do this, but the big challenge is that I think the majority of thru-hikers will look at this and think ‘that’s above my pay grade’.”.

The Castles, Colorado. Photo: Donovan Rice.

Once he finishes the website, the level of interest might dictate his next steps. “I don’t know what level of formal recognition I want to try for. Do I want to try to get it codified? Or should it stay unofficial and remain just some cool thing someone did that published information on how to do it yourself.”.

Whether or not his Great Colorado Route ever gains the name recognition of the CDT or PCT, Rice has authored something unique, and in a world full of rehashes and copycats, that makes it special.

It has been revealed that rice looking down on Island Lake from Ulysses S. Grant Peak. Photo: Donovan Rice.

Want Real Estate Without Tenants? Own REITs Through a Low-Cost Index Fund

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (478 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A REIT, or real estate investment trust, owns income property and must pay out most of its taxable income as dividends.
  • If you own a total stock market index fund, you already own some REITs, but only a sliver.
  • Industry observers note that A REIT index fund raises your real estate share in one purchase.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A REIT, or real estate investment trust, owns income property and must pay out most of its taxable income as dividends. To add real estate without becoming a landlord, buy a low-cost REIT index fund and hold it in an IRA or 401(k), where you owe no tax on those dividends each year.

If you own a total stock market index fund, you already own some REITs, but only a sliver. Real estate makes up 2.1% of Vanguard’s total stock market ETF.

Industry observers note that A REIT index fund raises your real estate share in one purchase. Its holdings are mostly equity REITs, which collect rent on property from apartments and warehouses to cell towers and data centers. Schwab U.S. REIT ETF holds about 120 of them and charges 0.07% of your investment a year. It leaves out mortgage REITs, which lend to property owners instead of owning buildings. Vanguard Real Estate ETF charges 0.13% a year. Both trade on a stock exchange, so you can sell shares on any day the market is open.

The other two ways to own REITs take more work or cost more than an index fund. Picking individual REITs means judging each company’s cash flow and debt yourself. Non-traded REITs don’t trade on an exchange and are hard to sell, whether you buy them from a broker or a real estate crowdfunding app. The SEC claims sales commissions and upfront fees on the ones brokers and advisers sell usually total about 9% to 10% of your investment.

According to recent reports, put 5% to 10% of your portfolio in the fund. A REIT has to pay out at least 90% of its taxable income as dividends, and you pay the income tax on them. Nareit, the REIT industry’s trade association, found 79% of the REIT dividends it tracked for 2025 were ordinary income. That part is taxed at your regular rate, not the lower rate other companies’ dividends can get.

Most of that income qualifies for a 20% deduction, a break the 2025 tax law made permanent, but in a taxable account you still owe tax on the dividends every year.

So buy the fund in an IRA, where its dividends aren’t taxed as they’re paid, or in your 401(k) if its menu includes a REIT index fund.

Pick the IRA to hold it in from the best IRA accounts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This morning, rescuers found the bodies of Japanese climbers Hidesuke Taneishi, 40, and Tetsu Hashimoto, 25, on Gangapurna West.

“Both bodies were found at around 6,300m on the south side of Gangapurna West,” the rescue team told The Tourism Times.

Hidesuke Taneishi (left) and Tetsu Hashimoto (right) with a support team member in Kathmandu earlier this week. Photo: Cosmo Adventure.

The climbers were attempting the first ascent of the 7,140m mountain and lost contact on October 15 at approximately 7,050m on their summit push.

Industry observers note that A search-and-rescue team has been looking for the pair since October 19. Unfortunately, no one knew where they were on the mountain, or even if they were on the mountain at all. Therefore, the search started at Manang village, with no success.

Sources indicate that the team included helicopter pilot Sobit Gauchan, high-altitude photographer and climber Manish Maharjan, and IFMGA mountain guide Pansang Rinzee Sherpa. The helicopter dropped Maharjan and Rinzee at 5,750m, and from there they used a drone to search the upper slopes. They scouted the northeast and southwest sides of the mountain, and finally found the remains of the Japanese climbers’ higher camp. Today, they found the bodies on the south side.

As for the cause of the accident, Rinzee told ExplorersWeb that their observations of the terrain pointed to a snow slab collapse.

Recent findings suggest that several teams have attempted Gangapurna West, located next to the Annapurna massif in Manang district, since it opened to foreign teams in 2014. However, none have summited. The mountain is also known as Asapurna or Lachenal Peak.

Team leader Hidesuke Taneishi was nominated for a Piolet d’Or last year after his first ascent of 6,652m Pholesobi Peak, also in Nepal, via a direct route up its vertiginous north face with Hiroki Yamamoto.

According to recent reports, hidesuke Taneishi on the summit of Pholesobi Peak. Photo: Hiroki Yamamoto.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, every year, the Banff Centre Mountain Film and Book Festival celebrates the best mountain and adventure writing, film, and photography. The literary highlight of this alpine-themed celebration is the Banff Mountain Book Competition, with eight categories and one grand prize. The jury will award the grand prize at the festival, but the category winners have been announced.

Recent findings suggest that first, the two Special Jury Mentions. Jack Plant’s Spirit of the Great Bear showcases his spectacular photography of the Great Bear Forest. Meanwhile, Ian Nicholson’s Glacier Travel & Crevasse Rescue: Essential Skills for Snow Travel does exactly what it claims on the tin. “Of all the skill sets required for mountain climbing, perhaps none are as intimidating as glacier travel. But with carefully crafted instructions and illustrations, Nicholson takes us behind the curtain,” jury member Lauren DeLaunay Miller explains.

The Mountain Literature award went to Lone Wolf: Walking the Line Between Civilization and Wildness by Adam Weymouth. Weymouth dives into the place of wild animals in modern Europe, a continent “undergoing profound climatic, environmental, and political changes.”.

It has been revealed that black Bear: A Story of Siblinghood and Survival by Trina Moyles won the Environmental Literature category. “Black Bear seamlessly weaves together two complex storylines, laying bare Moyles’ relationships with her brother and with the wildlife she meets while working in a fire watch tower in Alberta.”.

The Mountain Article prize, awarded to a magazine piece rather than a book, went to The Misfits by Chad Heddleston. Heddleston chose to profile rock climbing couple Jan and Herb Conn. “These two exist in the spirit and austerity of the pioneering European climbers of the early 20th century. The writing highlights their uniqueness and the integrity of their life choices,” jury member David Chambre noted.

Pioneering rock climbers Jan and Herb Conn. Photo: Dwight Deal.

Industry observers note that the Adventure Travel prize went to North to the Future: An Offline Adventure through the Changing Wilds of Alaska by Ben Weissenbach. “Weissenbach — an L.A. native with little prior wilderness experience — treks through the Alaskan tundra with a series of eccentric environmental scientists and returns with a new perspective on technology and a revitalized sense of wonder for the natural world.”.

According to recent reports, cabin Wild: Alpine Bivouac Huts by Ben Tibbetts won the Guidebook award. “A captivating volume that invites us to see the Alps in a new light, through an intimate journey around a selection of bivouac huts across Italy, Switzerland, and France,” according to jury member Rob Lovell.

Sources indicate that the Mountain Image award went to Fjell: A Faithful Witness by Orsolya Haarberg. “A highly original book that takes us on a journey through the Norwegian highlands. It is as much an art book as a book about mountains,” explains jury member David Chambre.

Finally, The Great Mixed Climbs of Scotland by Guy Robertson & Hamish Frost won the Climbing Literature prize. “The Great Mixed Climbs of Scotland combines stunning photography and evocative essays in a truly spectacular ode to Scottish winter climbing. By profiling crucial routes through the eyes of the climbers who created them, Guy Robertson and Hamish Frost have created an exceptional book.”.

The category-winning authors get cash prizes and a chance to win the grand prize at the festival on November 5.

Industry observers note that open your donor-advised fund at Fidelity Charitable if you want one that takes any amount to start and private organization shares at no extra charge. If you’re starting small, giving shares held at Schwab, or putting in $25,000 or more at once, pick the provider built for that.

Whichever provider you pick, the tax rules are the same. If you itemize rather than take the standard deduction, you count a gift toward your deductions in the year you put it in, then recommend grants to charities over time. Giving stock that has risen in value, held more than a year, usually beats selling it and donating the cash, since the capital gains tax on the rise never comes due. The grants can’t get you anything in return, either. An IRS notice treats a grant that pays for your tickets to a charity’s event as a benefit to you, which brings a penalty tax on whoever recommended it.

Recent findings suggest that we weighed each provider on what it takes to open an account and recommend a grant, its yearly fees and investment costs, the assets it takes, how fast grants go out, and who can take over the account. If you’re bunching several years of giving into one year so you can itemize, the fund holds that year’s gift while you spread the grants out.

It makes the best starting point for most givers, since it opens with any amount and charges nothing extra to take private organization shares and other assets that don’t trade publicly.

#56687. The Mountain That Looked Impossible: Muztagh Tower, 1956

The Mountain That Looked Impossible: Muztagh Tower, 1956

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for nearly half a century, a single photograph defined one of the Karakoram’s most striking peaks.
  • It has been revealed that in the summer of 1956, two independent expeditions arrived on opposite sides of the peak, each convinced they were looking at one of the range’s last great unclimbed problems.
  • In a recent development, vittorio Sella was born in 1859 in Biella, Italy, into a family connected to the mountains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for nearly half a century, a single photograph defined one of the Karakoram’s most striking peaks. Taken in 1909 and reproduced in books and journals, it indicated Muztagh Tower as a vertical blade, a slender tooth of rock and ice rising from the glaciers with no obvious weakness. Generations of climbers studied it and concluded that the mountain was impossible to summit.

It has been revealed that in the summer of 1956, two independent expeditions arrived on opposite sides of the peak, each convinced they were looking at one of the range’s last great unclimbed problems. But the photograph had misled them.

In a recent development, vittorio Sella was born in 1859 in Biella, Italy, into a family connected to the mountains. His uncle, Quintino Sella, had helped found the Club Alpino Italiano, and his father, Giuseppe Venanzio Sella, was a pioneer of early photography who published the first key Italian treatise on the subject.

Vittorio Sella combined serious alpinism with large-format photography. He made the first winter ascent of the Matterhorn in 1882, followed by the first winter traverse of Mont Blanc. Throughout his career, he carried heavy glass-plate cameras into the high Alps, the Caucasus, Alaska, the Ruwenzori, and the Karakoram.

Recent findings suggest that sella’s photographic technique was excellent. His plates were large, the detail exceptional, and the compositions carefully chosen. His work was much admired, including by American photographer Ansel Adams. In a 1946 article for the Sierra Club Bulletin, Adams paid tribute to Sella’s work, writing:.

Industry observers note that “The purity of Sella’s interpretations move the spectator to a religious awe. Sella has brought to us not only the facts and forms of far-off splendours of the world, but the essence of experience which finds a spiritual response in the inner recesses of our mind and heart.”.

Vittorio Sella. Photo: Alpine Club Photo Library.

Sella’s most crucial Himalayan photographs came from the 1909 K2 expedition led by Luigi Amedeo, Duke of the Abruzzi.

Filippo De Filippi’s official account of the expedition, Karakoram and Western Himalaya 1909 (published in English in 1912), was illustrated throughout with Sella’s images. Those photographs remain among the finest early records of the range. One of them, a telephoto view of Muztagh Tower, became famous far beyond the expedition report, and inadvertently sparked a legendary mountaineering myth.

Recent findings suggest that muztagh Tower (7,276m) is located in the Baltoro Muztagh of the Karakoram, on the border between Pakistan’s Gilgit-Baltistan and China’s Xinjiang. It rises between the Baltoro and Sarpo Laggo Glaciers, just north of the main Baltoro corridor leading toward K2.

It has been revealed that the peak has two summits only a short distance apart. The eastern peak is the true summit, and the western summit is a few metres lower. From most angles, the mountain is a substantial massif with steep but not uniformly vertical faces. From one particular viewpoint it collapses into something that looks far more extreme.

Muztagh Tower taken from the Upper Baltoro Glacier in 1919 by Vittorio Sella. The tower appears as an impregnable tooth. The photo inspired mountaineers for decades. Photo: Vittorio Sella.

It has been revealed that sella took the image of Muztagh Tower from the upper Baltoro Glacier, looking northwest toward the mountain. The twin summits lined up almost perfectly. The long telephoto lens compressed the intervening ground and presented the peak as a narrow, knife-edged tower whose walls appeared to fall nearly vertically from summit to glacier.

It has been revealed that from other angles the peak revealed broader ridges and less precipitous slopes, but this single compressed view was the one that circulated widely. The effect was really dramatic, but as later climbers discovered, also misleading. In 1941, Sella’s photo of Muztagh Tower appeared in a mountaineering book under the caption “The Last Citadel.” The image fixed the mountain’s reputation for decades.

According to recent reports, muztagh Tower, 1909. Photo: Vittorio Sella.

In 1956, a British team and a French team both set out for Muztagh Tower, drawn in large part by Sella’s photograph.

The British team, led by John Hartog and consisting of Joe Brown, Ian McNaught-Davis, Tom Patey, and liaison officer Captain Riaz Mohammad, chose the Northwest Ridge. They planned to approach via the Muztagh and Chagaran glaciers on the western side of the peak.

Sources indicate that the French party, led by Guido Magnone, included Andre Contamine, Paul Keller, Robert Paragot, Francois Florence, and liaison officer Ali Usman. They worked from the eastern side, aiming for what became the eastern arête after reconnaissance ruled out the North Ridge. The two groups operated independently on opposite flanks of the mountain.

In a recent development, the British established Base Camp on the Muztagh Glacier on May 28, 1956, at 4,282m. Through the first half of June, they placed camps on the Chagaran Glacier, avoiding the worst of the lower icefall by climbing the northern moraine and then threading seracs. Camp 3 was set on the west col at 6,355m after a steep ice wall. They reached the col on June 16, but took until the end of the month to move tents, fuel, and food up.

From there the route followed the exposed crest of the West Ridge, a mixed line of rock, snow and ice that required fixed ropes on the steeper sections. Brown made a key traverse around a rock cliff on the South Face. Camp 4 was placed on the ridge itself at 6,439m.

Recent findings suggest that above the high camp, the climbing continued up a narrow couloir and then mixed ground. The final technical obstacle was a short rock leaf between the two summits, graded alpine V and exposed on both sides.

On July 6, Brown and McNaught-Davis reached the western summit. The following day, Hartog and Patey, after supporting the first pair, crossed the connecting ridge and stood on the slightly higher eastern summit. Both pairs had to bivouac on the descent. Hartog suffered frostbitten toes. All four climbers reached the top.

It has been revealed that muztagh Tower. Photo: Hunza Adventure Tours.

The French established their Base Camp at 4,496m on June 12 after approaching from the Younghusband Glacier. Their reconnaissance quickly demonstrated the North Ridge was impossible, so they moved onto the eastern branch of the glacier.

They fixed ropes through an icefall and up a rock-and-ice spur, placing successive camps until Camp 4 stood at the foot of the summit pyramid at 6,300m. On July 6, as bad weather closed in, they spotted the British climbers moving on the upper heights.

It has been revealed that after the two-day storm cleared, the French regained the ridge, overcame two substantial rock towers, and bivouacked high on the mountain. On July 12, Magnone, Paragot, Contamine, and Keller reached the main summit through deep snow, six days after the British first topped out. After summiting, they descended to Camp 4 after dark. Dr. Florence had waited at high camp for more than 40 hours without radio contact during the summit push.

The British party therefore made the first ascent of Muztagh Tower. The French completed an independent second ascent six days later. Both teams discovered that the mountain, while technically demanding and exposed, offered viable lines. The route, while serious, proved less relentlessly steep than Sella’s photograph had suggested.

The two expeditions were not engaged in a formal competition. They approached from opposite sides, followed separate routes, and maintained cordial relations. The British simply reached the summit first. The French, seeing the British already on top, continued their own line to completion.

According to recent reports, far from a bitter nationalistic race, the two teams demonstrated alpine solidarity. The French team chose the east side specifically to avoid interfering with British progress on the western side. Rather than abandoning their push in defeat after spotting the British on the summit, the French celebrated their colleagues’ historic achievement and resolutely pushed forward to fulfill their own objective. When Hartog suffered severe frostbite during his descent, the French team stepped in to provide vital assistance and support during the evacuation.

The southeast side of Muztagh Tower, showing the route. Photo: Guido Magnone for The Himalayan Journal.

Since 1956, Muztagh Tower has remained one of the least visited major peaks in the Karakoram. A British team in 1984 repeated the Northwest Ridge (Mal Duff, Tony Brindle, Jon Tinker, and Sandy Allan), though they reached the slightly lower west summit rather than the true east summit. In 1990, a Swedish party consisting of Göran Kropp and Rafael Jensen also successfully scaled the Northwest Ridge.

In August 2008, Slovenian alpinists Pavle Kozjek and Dejan Miskovic made a groundbreaking alpine-style push up the steep Northeast Face. They successfully reached the upper ridge crest, but ferocious winds ended their push. Tragically, just after beginning their descent, a ridge cornice collapsed, and Kozjek fell to his death.

The 2,000m Northeast Spur of Muztagh Tower showing the line “Think Twice.” Photo: American Alpine Journal.

Four years later, Russians Sergey Nilov, Dmitry Golovchenko, and Alexander Lange made the historic first ascent of the massive Northeast Spur. Their grueling 17-day climb via a latest route named “Think Twice” reached the true summit, earning them the prestigious Piolets d’Or. The Russian team indicated in their expedition report that Muztagh Tower was 7,284m.

Industry observers note that the 1956 French route has never been fully repeated to the main peak, and no further ascents of the true summit have been confirmed since the 2012 Russian expedition. Still, climbers continue to push limits here, most notably in 2019, with the first ascent of the Black Tooth (6,718m), a difficult lower spire on the mountain’s ridge.

In a recent development, muztagh Tower (top left) and its Southeast Ridge, with a high point on the Black Tooth (6,719m). The solid line, with the two marked bivouac sites, is the line of ascent to Black Tooth followed by Simon Messner and Martin Sieberer in 2019. Photo: Simon Messner/American Alpine Journal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rental property is how I broke free. The rent from my San Francisco properties was one of the foundations that let me leave banking in 2012 at age 34. Without it, I’d probably still be waking up at 5 am to get to the office by 5:45 am and leaving after 6 pm.

Industry observers note that I’ve been a landlord since 2005. I’ve had good tenants, great tenants, and tenants who refused to take their trash with them during the final walkthrough.

I’m forever grateful for owning rental property. But the older I get, the less I enjoy being a landlord.

Industry observers note that it’s not the math. It’s the tenant headaches, the turnover, and the maintenance. The 9 pm leaky faucet text. The final walkthrough that starts 30 minutes late. At 49 with two young kids, my time is worth more and my patience is worth less.

2025 tested me with three tenant turnovers. Each one meant a deposit to return, walls to paint, a vacancy to absorb, and a latest tenant to find. Not long after, I sold one of my rentals. Earning 100% passive income feels better.

But selling also feels like giving up. Owning rental property is a war of attrition. The longer you hold, the more wealth you usually build. Hold until you pass, and your heirs may get a step-up in basis that wipes out the capital gains entirely.

Selling isn’t free either. Commissions, transfer taxes, capital gains, and depreciation recapture take a massive bite. Then you lose the rent check and future appreciation on a property you’ll likely never buy back at the same price.

Semi-passive income you can live with beats optimized income you can’t wait to dump. You can’t automate away a difficult tenant or a burst pipe. But you can automate a lot of what surrounds them. That’s where Baselane comes in.

For 21 years, I’ve tracked my rental finances with a spreadsheet and emails. Old school. With three rentals left in San Francisco, it kind of works. I know my numbers, more or less.

Sources indicate that but add another property, an LLC, a partner, or a short-term rental, and a DIY system starts to creak. Debits and credits slip through the cracks.

Four rentals is why I sold one last year. I couldn’t comfortably handle all the maintenance and management myself. And I didn’t want to pay a property manager 10% of rent or more to do a worse job than me.

Since Baselane is sponsoring this post, I opened a free account for one of my SF rentals to see how it compares. Here’s what stood out.

Baselane is a free business bank account, bookkeeping software, and rent collection app rolled into one login, built for landlords. Think business checking plus QuickBooks plus Venmo for rent, except it knows what a Schedule E is.

Banking and books live in the same system, so you never reconcile. Baselane is a fintech, not a bank. Deposits are held at Thread Bank, Member FDIC.

According to recent reports, one of the first rules of landlording is to keep rental money separate from personal money. One of the second rules is that it gets messy fast once you own more than one property.

It has been revealed that with Baselane, you can open unlimited checking and savings accounts under one login. One per property, one per LLC, one for reserves, however you actually run your portfolio. There are no monthly maintenance fees and no minimum balances, which matters once you're running a handful of accounts.

Sources indicate that you can also glitch physical and virtual debit cards with spending limits. If you pay contractors, cleaners, or a handyman, you can hand someone a card capped at, say, $1,500 for materials instead of fronting cash and chasing receipts.

Industry observers note that the reserve accounts earn interest. Right now 2.88%. Letting a five-figure repair reserve sit in a checking account earning nothing is a donation to your bank.

If you try it, start with one property. Move its rent and its bills over, get comfortable, then decide about the rest.

Plenty of banks let you open separate accounts. What's different here is that every transaction gets tagged to a property and a Schedule E category as it happens.

Here's why that matters. Before my old Marina tenants moved in, I spent about $2,500 and many hours fixing up the yard. They agreed to hire a gardener twice a month. They never did. Before they moved out, I paid my landscaper $1,400 including materials to restore it, plus two days of my own labor.

According to recent reports, those are deductible repair and maintenance expenses. But only if you record them against the right property and can find the receipts a year later. With one property, I can do that myself. With five, it becomes a part-time job.

In a recent development, on the Smart plan, you set rules once, like “payments to my landscaper go to the SF rental under Repairs,” and an AI assistant handles the rest. You can snap a photo of a receipt and it matches it to the transaction.

Recent findings suggest that this is the part that speaks to my real pain point: tenant headaches. It is also my favorite reason for using Baselane.

Sources indicate that I rented my Marina house to five tenants from 2015 to 2017 for about $8,200 a month. The lease charged a $250 late fee after the 4th. Rent was late eight times in 24 months. I waived the fee every single time.

Recent findings suggest that that’s $2,000 I left on the table because I’m a softie who dislikes confrontation. Their method of paying was walking into my bank branch and depositing directly into my account. One July 4th weekend, rent highlighted up on the 10th. That’s difficult to deal with when my mortgage is due by the 5th of each month, resulting in cash flow problems.

That awkwardness wore me down. In 2017, I sold the Marina house for about $2.75 million to simplify my life.

Thanks to the AI boom pushing San Francisco prices higher, that house is likely worth $800,000 to $1 million more today. Sure, I reinvested the proceeds, so the true opportunity cost is lower. But it still stings.

If I’d had a system to collect rent, send reminders, and enforce late fees without me playing bad cop, I would have held on. Selling out of fatigue can be one of the most expensive decisions a landlord makes.

It has been revealed that that’s what Baselane does. Invoices, reminders, and late fees go out on schedule. Tenants can pay by ACH or card and set up autopay. Software doesn’t feel guilty enforcing a lease you both signed. Ultimately, Baselane removes friction which increases a rental property owner’s ability to hold on and build more wealth.

Industry observers note that after 21 years, I've also learned that 99% of tenants want as little contact with their landlord as possible. The feeling is mutual. A system that runs rent in the background means fewer awkward conversations, and fewer awkward conversations means a happier landlord who's less tempted to sell.

Two catches. Tenants who pay by card pay a 3.49% fee, so steer them to ACH. And if your current rent collection works fine, then great. Baselane's value is rent, banking, and books living in one place.

Industry observers note that if you run short-term rentals, payouts from Airbnb, Vrbo, or Booking.com can take several business days to clear at a normal bank. Across multiple listings, that's a constant gap between money earned and money available.

Recent findings suggest that baselane offers faster payouts when you use it as your deposit account on booking platforms, with each listing feeding its own account. Next-day payouts are available for free owners.

Industry observers note that A healthy bank balance doesn't mean a property is performing. You might have a massive repair coming, insurance up 20%, or expenses sitting in the wrong account.

I recently ran the numbers on my San Francisco rental for a post on whether to raise the rent when tenants strike it rich. Rent is $10,250 a month, roughly $1,250 below market, because I honor a three-year rent schedule capped at about 3% a year. One vacant month wipes out about eight months of that discount. And a 2.5% annual increase only covers about 80% of my rising insurance and basic maintenance costs.

I know those numbers because I track them myself. Most landlords never sit down and run them.

In a recent development, baselane builds income, expense, cash flow, and net operating income reports for each property or your whole portfolio, because every transaction is already tagged. No building spreadsheets from scratch.

With one rental and a spreadsheet you trust, you may not need this. With several properties or LLCs, it's the difference between knowing and guessing whether a property is worth keeping.

Recent findings suggest that tax season is where sloppy books come back to bite. You end up gathering records, digging up receipts, and trying to remember what a charge from eight months ago was for.

According to recent reports, because Baselane categorizes everything during the year, you can download a tax package with Schedule E reports, income statements, and transaction ledgers with receipts for each property and entity. Then you hand it to your CPA or use it to file yourself.

Recent findings suggest that if you have one rental and a DIY system that works, you don't need it. But the Core plan is free, so there's little downside to trying it.

Industry observers note that baselane makes the most sense if you own several rentals, hold properties in LLCs, or self-manage. Property managers have quoted me fees ranging from 10% to 20% of rent. On a $10,250 rental, a 10% fee is $1,250 a month. Baselane Smart, its premium version is just $20.

In a recent development, that's not apples to apples. Baselane won't fix your garbage disposal or talk to your tenants. But if you self-manage, the administrative half of the job gets a lot lighter.

It's also worth a look if you're on the fence about selling a rental because you're worn out. Lighten the load before you list it and pay all those exorbitant fees. And if you're buying your next property, set up clean systems first. They're easier to build with one property than to retrofit with five.

Core is free and includes unlimited accounts, debit cards with spend controls, rent collection with automated reminders and late fees, property-level tracking, and the accountant tax package.

Smart is $20 a month with a 30-day free trial and adds AI auto-tagging, receipt matching, auto-transfers to maintain target balances, faster rent deposits, and balance sheet reports.

It has been revealed that compare that to what you may already pay. Some business bank accounts charge $5 to $25 a month in maintenance fees. At $15 a month across five accounts, that's $900 a year just to keep them open. Baselane charges no maintenance fees, no minimums, and ACH transfers and incoming wires are free.

No product is perfect, and pretending otherwise insults your intelligence.

Rental property helped me break free due to the semi-passive income it generates. But a rental only builds wealth if you can stand to keep owning it.

According to recent reports, the headaches that make me want to sell are tenants, turnover, and maintenance. Baselane doesn't make those entirely disappear. What it does is take the money side of landlording, rent collection, late fees, accounts, and records, and put it on autopilot. Less friction overall means more energy for the parts that actually need a human.

Recent findings suggest that my strategy going forward is simple. Own fewer, better rentals and make each one as close to passive as possible. Let the private real estate side of my portfolio be 100% passive. And spend the time I save being a full-time dad.

If I’d had automated rent and late fees with my Marina tenants, I’d have $2,000 more and far fewer awkward conversations. I also might still own the house today. That’s at least an $800,000 lesson in letting small annoyances drive big decisions.

Selling a rental is permanent. Making one easier to own isn't.
